en: Śrī Oṃ. Salutations to that Brahman which is Tat-Sat. Now begins the Rasaratnasamuccaya.

The First Chapter: On the Production of the Essence (Rasotpatti) Salutation to that Supreme Physician, the foremost in the world, by whose manifestation as bliss— which is endowed with the auspicious arts, which is a throbbing splendor, which is the nectar of perfected essence, and which is an ocean of the nectar of compassionate glances— the diseases of birth, destruction, old age, passion, and so forth are instantly pacified for his devotees.
Ādiman, Candrasena, the skilled Laṅkeśa,
Kapālī, Mattamāṇḍavya, Bhāskara, and Śūrasenaka.
Ratnakośa, Śambhu, Sāttvika, Naravāhana,
Indrada, Gomukha, Kambali, and Vyāḍi.
Nāgārjuna, Surānanda, Nāgabodhi, Yaśodhana,
Khaṇḍa, Kāpālika, Brahmā, Govinda, Lampaka, and Hari.
There are twenty-seven [tantras] in number that bestow the accomplishment of mercury (rasasiddhi):
Rasāṅkuśa, Bhairava, Nandī, and Svacchandabhairava; 1.5.
Manthānabhairava, Kākacaṇḍīśvara, Vāsudeva, the sage Śṛṅga, and the compiler of the Kriyātantrasamuccaya; VRrs_1.6 //
The Yogin Rasendratilaka, Bhālukī, he who is called Maithila,
Mahādeva, Narendra, Vāsudeva, and Harīśvara.
Having examined other tantras, this compendium is now composed for the sake of those perfected elixirs (rasas) that are useful for medical treatment. 1.8.
The *Rasaratnasamuccaya* was composed by the son of Siṃhagupta;
it treats mercury, the secondary minerals, metals, and the various instruments and procedures.
For the purpose of purifying metals, the methods for forging and so forth will be explained;
purification, essence, liquefaction, and the production of ash shall now be described.
In the northern direction, there is a great mountain, a dwelling of mist,
whose mass of lofty peaks has surpassed the clouds.
Exhausted by the intense fatigue of traversing the path through the sky,
the host of autumnal clouds descended, as it were, to the earth for rest.
It shines forth, exceedingly lofty, as if it had emerged from the earth after piercing through it— the mass of light from the hoods of the lord of the serpent-chiefs who dwell in the zodiac signs.
The gem-studded grounds of its slopes, with their glowing medicinal herbs,
imitate the clouds at night with their unrestrained flashes of lightning.
In his mountain fastness, as the Kinnara women moved about,
the application of lac-dye was performed upon their feet by means of mineral pigments.
Adorned with the cool-rayed moon as his crest-ornament, his naked body veiled by the directions,
he who dwells in the cave is celebrated by the world as Girīśa.
Upon whose peaks the sages, with eyes perpetually closed,
perceive Giriśa, who is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
By the spray of its waterfalls, which strikes against surfaces of stone,
the Yakṣas perceive the sky, marked by stars, even during the day.
In that place, where men are unable to endure the intensity of the frosty winds,
they constantly seek the warmth of their own wives' breasts.

As he wandered through the mountain fastnesses, even in the heat of summer, the sun’s fierce warmth was blocked by intense frost so that it could not distinguish itself from the cool rays of the moon.
In mountain caves fragrant with musk from the navel of the kastūri deer,
where kinnarīs sing of the wedding festival of Gaurī.
There shines Maheśvara, the primordial god of the worlds;
for he was born as Mahārasa in the form of Rasa (the essence) in order to protect the universe.
The merit that men obtain from performing a hundred horse-sacrifices, from giving a thousand pieces of gold,
or from bathing at all sacred fords, is attained by the mere sight of one who has undergone childbirth impurity (sūtaka).
Whoever, endowed with devotion, having fashioned a *rasaliṅga*, should worship it,
shall obtain the fruit of worshipping all the *liṅgas* of the three worlds.
Consuming, touching, giving, meditating, and fully worshipping—
these fivefold offerings of nectar are said to destroy even the greatest sins.
By the mere act of eating it, one destroys the entire multitude of diseases arising from the sins of previous births for all men; there is no doubt in this matter.
The sins committed by embodied beings in previous births perish instantly if Śambhu is anointed with the paste of fragrant powder.
"Whoever thoroughly digests even a mere *truṭi* of mica within the mercury, for him there shall be the fruit of a hundred sacrifices; thus spoke Śiva."
And whoever reviles the Lord of Sūtas, the supreme radiance of Śambhu,
shall fall into a terrible hell for as long as the duration of a kalpa.
He who gives medicinal juice, properly prepared through purification and cooking, to the sick,
obtains the eternal fruit of the Tulā-dāna and the Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Once the elixir is perfected, I shall make the world free from the disease of poverty;
this meditation on the elixir has been proclaimed as the remover of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
For the consumption of mercury by clouds is proclaimed as the sacrificial offering (naivedya) for the essence;
having performed this worship of the rasa, one shall obtain the fruit born of sacrifice.
When the child is situated in the womb and his life departs,
he is liberated from terrible evil and proceeds to the supreme state.
Having fainted, it removes disease; having experienced bondage, it becomes the giver of liberation;
indeed, having died, it makes one immortal—what other source of compassion is there besides mercury?

Since he pacifies even that leprosy— which is indeed incurable and arises from the mass of sins committed by harming the preceptors of the gods, cows, and the twice-born— who, then, is more pure than the Sūta?
Only the binding of mercury is blessed, for at its very commencement there is the constant thought:
"When the mercury is perfected, I shall make the earth free from old age and death. (VR 1.36)

This birth in a noble family is indeed the fruit of well-performed deeds; moreover, there is wisdom even therein, and that wisdom has as its fruit the ability to weigh the entire surface of the earth, while the earth itself is easily governed.
The fruits of subjugating the earth are material objects, and those yield various kinds of enjoyment as their fruit;
yet enjoyments exist only within the body, which is therefore impermanent—hence, all of it is in vain.
Thus, considering wealth, the body, and enjoyments to be impermanent, one must always strive for liberation;
that [liberation] comes from knowledge, that [knowledge] from practice, and that [practice] when the body is stable.

No alchemical elixir (rasāyana), such as mercury or base metals, is capable of ensuring stability in that [state], for it is itself unstable by nature, combustible, subject to moisture, and liable to dry up. (VR 1.40)
Wooden plants dissolve into lead; lead into tin, and tin into copper;
copper into silver, silver into gold, and gold dissolves into mercury.
Just as yogins, when dissolved within the form of Hara, attain immortality,
so too do gold, iron, and other metals [attain it] when the sky is swallowed by the king of essences (rasarāja).
Just as in the Supreme Self, there is a constant dissolution of all sentient beings therein;
this unique king of essences makes the body free from old age and death.
Having attained knowledge endowed with the eight qualities through the power of practice while the body remains stable,
one reaches the state of Brahman and no longer experiences the sufferings of birth or dwelling in rebirth.
The supreme light stands pervading the entire world simultaneously with one quarter;
that immortal state is easily attained through the other three quarters, not by mere detachment alone.
For it is not possible by means of this body— which is afflicted by the sufferings of disease, old age, and death,
and which perishes in an instant— to worship that subtle Brahman in any way whatsoever.
Who would utter even the name of one who has attained perfection of the body without that body itself—
that reality which is accessible through yoga, stainless, and beyond the range of even the mind?
It is said that through sacrifice, charity, austerity, the study of the Vedas, self-restraint, and virtuous conduct,
self-realization arises most abundantly indeed by the power of yoga.
Situated between the two eyebrows, that supreme light consisting of consciousness— which illuminates the world like fire, lightning, and the sun—
manifests for those whose vision is purified by merit.

It is the single essence of supreme bliss, the nature of the highest light, free from conceptual construction, with all afflictions dissolved; it is the object of knowledge, peaceful, and to be personally realized.
Fixing the mind upon that [Self], seeing the entire throbbing world as consisting of consciousness,
one whose bonds of karma are destroyed attains the state of Brahman even here in this life.
Freed from passion and hatred, practicing truth and devoid of falsehood,
they become indistinguishable in all respects through contact with the Consciousness-Brahman.
They remain endowed with the powers such as *aṇimā*, their bodies radiant, ever-arisen in bliss;
having attained the immortal nature of Brahman, they have indeed accomplished all that was to be done.
Abandoning this one body alone, which is the abode of sciences and the root of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— what other supreme good could there be than this, which is free from old age and death?
How can one who does not know of birth (sūtaka) through the means of direct perception (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa) know the God who consists of consciousness, whose form is invisible?
That which is worn out by old age and rendered helpless by the sufferings of cough, asthma, and the like,
is unfit for meditative concentration, as it obstructs the functioning of the intellect and the senses.
How can a mortal man— first a child of sixteen years, addicted to relishing the flavors of sensory objects,
then one whose discernment has passed away, and finally an old man— attain liberation?
For those who have no realization of the Supreme Self within this very body,
that Brahman is even more remote for them after the abandonment of the body.
Brahmā and the other gods strive for that [state], having assumed divine bodies;
so too do others who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta), as well as sages who endure until the end of the kalpa.
Therefore, a yogi desiring liberation while living must first assume a divine body through the union of the creation of Hara and Gaurī.
On this mountain, as Śiva and Śivā engaged in sexual union out of mutual affection and a desire to conquer one another— an act that caused the three worlds to tremble— (61)
Desiring a son who would be the slayer of the demon Tāraka, the gods dispatched the Fire-god to prevent their sexual union.
In a cave of the Himalayas, he encountered Anala in the form of a pigeon;
agitated by his loss of wings, he gazed upon her with the playful movements of love.
Seeing him, Śambhu was ashamed and then desisted from the act of love;
the final emission was released and caught by the wielder of the trident.
He was cast into the mouth of the Fire-god and fell even into the Gaṅgā;
yet she too, being scorched all over, threw him back out.
From the depositing of that impurity, the bodily constituents (dhātus) were produced as the causes of accomplishment,
until the semen fell from the mouth of Agni due to its great essence.
Having made those five wells each one hundred yojanas deep,
from that time forward his semen remained within the wells, divided into five parts.
Rasa, Rasendra, Sūta, Pārada, and likewise Miśraka—
thus the fivefold [mercury] born from Śambhu arises according to the distinction of its source-places (kṣetra).
The essence (rasa), red in color, was released, free from all defects, serving as an elixir (rasāyana).
By means of it, the thirty gods (tridaśas) were born, free from disease, devoid of decay, and immortal.
The lord of mercury, when freed from its impurities, becomes dark, dry, and extremely volatile;
by means of it, the practitioners of alchemy became like serpents, liberated from death and old age.
The gods and the nāgas filled those two wells with earth and stones;
from that time forward, they became exceedingly difficult for people to find.
Slightly yellowish in hue, with a dry body, and endowed with the [proper] qualities, that mercury (sūtaka),
perfected through eighteen refinements, transforms the body into iron.
Now, there is another, mobile substance produced from a well, white in color, which is mercury;
for it removes all diseases through various medicinal preparations.
That rasa, possessing the luster of a peacock’s eye, is considered *miśraka*;
when endowed with the eighteen refinements, it grants exceedingly great success.
The three beginning with the Sūta— the Sūtas and so forth— though they bring about all accomplishments,
possess power in an extreme degree through the manifestations of their own specific karmas.
He who understands this production of tastes is righteous;
he attains longevity, health, progeny, and the perfection of tastes.
Because it is the essence of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), it is called "rasa";
or rather, it is considered *rasa* because it is tasted for the destruction of old age, disease, and death.
Because it is the king of tastes and the sovereign of juices, it is celebrated as *rasendra*;
because it produces the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the body and of metals, it is therefore known as *sūta*.
He is called *pārada* because he delivers those submerged in the mire and ocean of disease;
he is that in which the luster residing in all minerals remains, intermingled with fire.
Therefore, that [mercury] is called "mixed" (miśraka), bestowing fruits of various forms.
By the power of such mercury— which severs the death and disease of mortals—
human beings have come to possess strength and lifespan equal to those of the gods.
Having seen them, Rudra was immediately entreated by Śakra;
and the king of essences (mercury) was then joined with the defects and the casings.
From that time forward, this charioteer, being unrefined, did not attain perfection;
though moving upon the water in the form of water, he swiftly became one who goes like a swan.
The impure goes by way of impurity, and the smoky becomes one who goes by way of smoke;
the divine course of the living being is another, whereby the soul emerges as if from an egg.
He gives life to those living beings; therefore, the vital essence (rasa) is known as "life" (jīva).
Four states of existence are visible, while the fifth state is invisible.
By means of mantra, meditation, and so forth, his fifth destiny is obstructed.
Thus, because the course of the king of elixirs is so varied, its purification is difficult to achieve;
nevertheless, a skilled physician should protect it.
Seeing the bride, well-adorned and mounted upon a horse, having bathed after her first menses and looking about, the nectar situated in the well desired to seize her.
Seeing him, she too rose up with speed and departed with great velocity;
the charioteer followed her for a distance of one yojana to the boundary.
Then Śiva’s son returned to the well with speed;
they caught the mercury as it rested in the hollows dug along the path.
It fell into the Darada region due to its weight from the fiery mouth.
That essence, having dissolved into the earth, is extracted as mercury by the inhabitants of various regions who place that clay into a distillation apparatus (pātanāyantra).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of Mercury," in the *Rasaratnasamuccaya*, composed by the teacher Vāgbhaṭa, son of the lord of physicians Siṃhagupta.
Now begins the second chapter: [The Great Tastes].
Abhra, vaikrānta, mākṣika, vimala, ādrija, and sasyaka;
Having understood that there are eight types of mercury, including the restless (capala) and the liquid (rasaka), one should collect them.
"The goddess's *rajas* becomes the fragrance, and the element *śukra* likewise becomes *abhraka*"; this is an interpolated verse.
The supreme nectar of Gaurī’s luster destroys wind, bile, and wasting diseases; it awakens wisdom, pacifies ailments, and is the foremost aphrodisiac and life-prolonging tonic.

It is strengthening, unctuous, appetizing, increases *kapha*, stimulates digestion, and is cool in potency; through various formulations, it cures all diseases, and like the sky, it binds the lord of mercury (*sūtendra*).
That solid earth which is brought from a depth below the king’s cubit in the excavation shall yield the aforementioned results; however, that which is devoid of essence is utterly fruitless.
Pināka, Nāgamaṇḍūka, and Vajra—these are considered the types of abhraka;
each of these is fourfold according to the distinction of colors such as white and so forth.
The Pināka bow, heated by fire, releases a mass of arrows;
having bound the impurity accumulated through its service, it surely kills the man.
One should produce a sound like that of a serpent while remaining within the fire;
by consuming that, one undoubtedly contracts the skin disease known as maṇḍala-kuṣṭha.
By repeatedly leaping up, a frog causes the stone to swell and fall;
this produces the disease of urinary calculi (aśmarī), which is incurable except by surgical means.
Vajrābhra (diamond-ore), when heated in fire until it is freed from all its impurities, produces a body and iron; it is the supreme remover of all diseases.
It is of four kinds: white, red, yellow, and black.
White is prescribed for white rites; that which has a reddish luster is for red rites;
and that abhraka which has a yellow luster is the best for yellow rites.
Although four kinds of excellent space are mentioned in the science of alchemy (rasāyana),
nevertheless, black-colored cloud-like [space] possesses millions upon millions of times more qualities.
Glossy, with broad leaves, endowed with excellent color, and heavier than the *bhārata* variety;
with leaves that are easy to strip away—that cloud is declared to be the most auspicious.
The mercury shall not swallow the sky, which resembles dross and is accompanied by moonlight;
once swallowed, however, it should be employed in both metallurgy and alchemy.
One should resort to the moonless, dead sky during the periods of creation;
and when it is served while joined with the moon, one should practice the slow digestion of urine.
Those who, devoid of reason, have spoken of leaf-minerals as an elixir,
have surely seen the poison known as *kālakūṭa* intended for the purpose of sustaining life.
For the sake of sentient beings and for the sake of service, one should employ purified abhraka;
otherwise, having rendered it devoid of its qualities, it will certainly cause harm.
Abhra heated seven times and placed in sour gruel (kāñjika),
or even cast into cow's urine, certainly becomes free from defects.
Furthermore, having prepared *dhānyābhraka* in cow’s milk boiled with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), one should grind it with the juices of *matsyākṣikā*.
Having formed it into a pill and dried it, one should then roast it in an *ardhabhaka* crucible;
indeed, one should roast it in this manner six times with the juice of *punarnavā*.
Having ground it even with a sixteenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa and formed it into pills,
one should indeed roast it seven times using the *ardhebhaka*-type crucibles.
In this manner, one should also saturate it seven times with the juice of vāsā and the juice of taṇḍulīya, according to the procedure previously described.
Thus, one should employ the perfected *ghana* in all yogic practices.
Powdered mica combined with rice and bound in cloth is placed in sour gruel (kāñjika);
when it has emerged from the cloth due to rubbing, it is called dhānyābhra.
Rice-mercury (dhānyābhra), thoroughly rubbed with the juice of Kāsamarda and subjected to ten cycles of heating in a closed crucible (puṭapāka), is killed; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, with the juice of *mustā* and the juice of *taṇḍulīya*,
one should grind auspicious *āmalaka* and *abhraka* (mica) that has been fashioned into discs.
When processed by being folded sixty times, it becomes the color of vermilion;
it destroys all diseases beginning with consumption when used as a medicine for illnesses.
By means of decoctions of the bark from the root of a banyan tree, or from the essence of betel leaves, or with vāsā and matsyākṣikā, or with mīnākṣī and kaṭillā; VRs 2.27.
When the thick [substance] of the *vaṭa* tree is rubbed with milk and processed in a closed crucible twenty times, it will acquire a luster like that of vermilion.
Combined with one-fourth part of ṭaṅkaṇa and rubbed with the juice of musalī, it should be sealed in a crucible and strongly heated;
it will become wealth in the form of essence (sattva).
And separately with the juices of *kāsamarda*, *ghana*, *dhvāna*, *vāsā*, *punarnavā*, *matsyākṣī*, *kāṇḍavallī*, and *haṃsapādī*.
Having ground [the ingredients] repeatedly with effort, one should dry them according to the application of heat;
[one part] of wheat flour, small fish, and borax, each weighing one *pala*.
Having added one-eighth part of each [ingredient] repeatedly, one should grind them;
after each grinding, one should properly dry the mixture with the rays of the sun.
Having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or the five products of the goat (*pañcāja*), or likewise the five products of the buffalo (*pañcamāhiṣa*),
one should fashion cow-dung balls slightly larger than the size of a *tinduka* fruit.
Milk, curd, ghee, urine, and dung are said to be derived from the goat;
having blown [the crucible] in a downward-dropping furnace, one should cause the essence (sattva) to fall out.
Having collected the dross from within the crucible and reduced it to powder, one should extract the metallic globules;
then, having ground that dross with a small amount of borax and cow dung.
Having formed balls and dried them again in the heat as before,
one should once more collect the dross (kiṭṭa), crush it, and extract the essence (sattva).
Then, having boiled those seeds of *sattva* with sour *kāñjika*,
and having enclosed them within a crucible together with the group of purifying substances, one should seal it shut.
Having properly melted it and collected it, one should heat the metal twice;
thus the sattva becomes pure and may be employed in alchemy and rejuvenation therapies.
When a hard substance such as iron is melted and poured ten times into honey, oil, fat, or clarified butter, it becomes soft.
Then, having prepared cotton-seed powder and thoroughly saturated it with cow's ghee,
one should fry it seven times in a pan placed upon a stove.
One should grind it again and again until it becomes the color of fire;
or one should perform the roasting until, when a blade of grass is thrown upon it, it burns.
Then, having ground it together with sulphur, one should roast it twenty times using a Vārāha-puṭa (pig-shaped crucible) with a decoction of the roots of the *vaṭa* tree.
Furthermore, [he should drink] twenty times from a decoction made of the three myrobalans (triphalā),
along with muṇḍikā, bhṛṅgarāja leaves, pathyā, and the roots of akṣa.
Having prepared it, it should be administered in the proper dose for all diseases;
there is nothing else superior to *sattva* (mercury) in being free from adverse effects and possessing greater therapeutic qualities.
If prepared in this manner by means of a hundred-fold *puṭapāka* cooking,
it becomes exceedingly endowed with qualities, acting as a supreme digestive and appetizer.

Bastard myrobalan leaves, processed with jaggery and the juice of *gandharva* leaves, [cure] hemorrhoids above and below; and *tripuṭa* [leaves], processed with the juice of *vaṭa* leaves, [cure] piles.
By consuming it in a dose of half a *guñjā* seed, it produces excessive hunger;
yet, through formulations that alleviate specific diseases, it is the supreme remedy for all diseases.
The ball of *sattva* should be blown [into a flame] and quenched instantly in *kāñjika* mixed with grain; then one should grind it with an iron pestle.
Having heated it and cast thick, large droplets into sour gruel (kāñjika),
one should collect them immediately, crush them, and prepare the powder.
And one should fry that powder three times with cow’s ghee as before,
or likewise with the juice of *dhātrī* fruits or with the juice of *dhātrī* leaves.
The grinding should be done repeatedly with a stone slab and a pestle;
then, it should be treated again with the juices of *punarnavā* mixed with *kāñjika*.
One should roast it ten times and [fumigate] it ten times with fragrant substances;
thus purified, the essence of *vyoma* (mercury) possesses all supreme qualities.
It may be employed as desired for the process of digestion (*jāraṇa*) and for alchemy (*rasāyana*).
Although various fluxes (*druti*) have been firmly observed and taught in the scriptures,
they never succeed without the grace of Śambhu.
Divyābhra, when consumed in a dose of one ball (valla) combined with *vellaja*, *vyoṣa*, and clarified butter, overcomes consumption, anemia, dysentery, colic,
skin diseases, wasting, asthma, urinary disorders, loss of appetite, difficult-to-cure cough, weak digestion, abdominal pain, and indeed all diseases through its medicinal formulations.
Now, regarding vaikrānta:
that which is eight-sided, has eight facets, is hexagonal, smooth, and heavy,
and is endowed with pure or mixed colors, is called vaikrānta.
White, red, yellow, blue,
the color of a pigeon, dark, black, and variegated— thus he is indeed eightfold.
It bestows longevity, produces strength and complexion, is highly aphrodisiac, grants wisdom, removes all humors and diseases,
kindles the digestive fire, possesses qualities equal to those of nectar, and is full of vitality.
Vaikrāntaka indeed bestows physical strength and produces iron.
In all elixirs (*rasāyana*), the powerful *vaikrānta*, which is to be ranked first, should be employed in place of diamond (*vajra*); it removes all defects.
[In another text it is said: "The lord of the Daityas, Mahiṣa, who was born from Sahadeva, was crushed by the Blessed Goddess Durgā with her trident. (VR 2.59)
Wherever his blood fell upon the earth and remained there,
in those very places there appeared vaikrānta, a great mineral in the form of a diamond.
It exists to the south or to the north of the Vindhya mountains, or indeed everywhere;
it cuts through metals, and for that reason it is known as vaikrāntaka.
White, yellow, red, blue, and the color of a pigeon;
another like the neck of a peacock, and one with the luster of emerald.
Black [mercury] brings about the perfection of the body; yellow [mercury] when yellow, and white [mercury] when white;
red [mercury] grants success in all aims, as does that which has the luster of emerald.
The remaining two are fruitless and should be avoided; thus, vaikrānta is of seven kinds.
Now, the procedure for collection:
Having worshipped Bhairava and Vināyaka in the field where the vaikrānta is situated, one should take it with a pure mind.
Vaikrānta is considered to be like a diamond; it bestows strength upon the body and produces iron, destroys poison, is the king of mercury, and cures fever, leprosy, and consumption.
Vaikrāntaka stones become purified after three days when they have been steamed while being treated with alkaline salts,
or cooked in sour liquids, urine, the water of horse-gram, plantain, or kodrava grain.
Vaikrānta is purified when steamed in a decoction of kulattha;
it is killed by eight applications of heat when combined with the juice of gandhanimbuka.
And when the *vaikrānta* stones have been heated, one should pour horse urine over them;
or one may do this repeatedly, providing liquid and then applying the *puṭa* seal.
One should employ reduced-to-ashes *vaikrānta* in place of *vajra*,
having processed it with the alkalis of *mokṣa*, *morata*, and *pālāśa*, and with cow urine.
Combined with the paste of *vajrakanda* and *niśā*, along with the powder of its fruit,
that paste, borax, lac-powder, and that which is produced from *vaikrānta*.
Combined with *navasāra* and mixed with the juice of *meṣaśṛṅgī*,
it is formed into a ball, placed in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), and heated with a fierce fire.
In that very [process], the essence (sattva) of vaikrānta falls out, without a doubt.
Having been ground by means of the yoga for precipitating the essence and made into a pill,
the vaikrānta placed in a crucible and heated for one ghaṭikā will release its essence.

Vikṛtaka, having attained the state of ash and combined with one-quarter part of dead gold (mercury), along with *kaṇā*, clarified butter, and *vellaja*, when consumed in the measure of a *guñjā*, conquers consumption, indigestion, jaundice, hemorrhoids, asthma, cough, malignant *grahaṇī*, chest wounds, and other diseases; it is a creator of bodily vigor.
The ash of blue vaikrānta combined with half its amount of iron-pigment ash (sūtabhasman),
along with an equal quantity of the essence of dead mica, should be thoroughly rubbed together.
If one consumes a dose the size of a *guñjā* seed, combined with honey and clarified butter, in the morning,
it destroys all diseases that are difficult to overcome by other medicines;
in twenty-one days, it removes [diseases] just as the waters of the Gaṅgā wash away sins.
Now, regarding honey:
the golden nectar produced from the Golden Mountain was fashioned by Viṣṇu in Tāpyā, among the Kirātas, the Cīnas, and the Yavanas.
In the month of Mādhava, when heated by the rays of the sun, it is seen to be sweet and golden-hued; when sour, it resembles silver.
Slightly astringent and sweet, cold, pungent in its post-digestive effect, and light;
by its consumption, one is not overcome by old age, disease, or poisons.
Mākṣika is of two kinds: hemamākṣika and tāramākṣika.
Among these, the first type of mākṣika originates from Kānyakubja and resembles gold in appearance.
That which is produced on the banks of the Tapatī, resembling gold of five colors, is said to be the stone-abundant variety known as *tāra*; it possesses few qualities.
Mākṣika mineral destroys all diseases, is indeed the very life-force of mercury (rasendra), and is supremely aphrodisiac;
it effects the fusion of the two metals that are otherwise difficult to combine, possesses superior qualities, and is the foremost among all elixirs (rasāyana).
Honey purified by boiling it with castor oil, citron juice,
and water, or boiled for two ghaṭikās with the juice of plantain roots, becomes pure.
Honey attains purity when heated and cast into a decoction of *varā*,
then ground with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and *gandhā*, and placed inside a crucible.
Honey indeed dies when burnt five times with the folds of a *kroḍa* leaf,
using either castor oil, cow's fat, or the juice of *mātuluṅga*.
When firmly cooked in a crucible, it becomes as hard as a metal;
thus, once killed, it may be employed in alchemy (rasāyana) as well as in the preparation of mercury.
Combined with one-thirtieth part of nāga and processed with alkaline and acidic substances,
the mākṣika ore, when smelted in an open crucible, releases its essence.
Having been stirred seven times and cast into the juice of *nirguṇḍī*,
lead mixed with the essence of honey will certainly be destroyed.
Honey processed repeatedly with the oils of gandharva and kṣaudra, with cow’s urine, with ghee, and with the essence of the root of the plantain tree; VRs 2.89.
When heated in a crucible, it releases its essence, which is soft and resembles copper.
Having a luster like the seed of the *guñjā* plant, melting when heated and cooling down,
that purified essence of *tāpya* (calamine) is supreme for producing a body of iron.
Having ground the mercury with the essence of honey, and having placed the offering into it once it has melted,
one should mix and rub it together in the middle of a mortar, adding the essence and the liquefied mica.
Having formed a pill in a vessel called *lavaṇayantra*, one should cook it for half a day over a mild fire.
Once it has cooled naturally, one should thoroughly powder it and take a dose of one *valla* combined with *vyoṣa* and *viḍaṅga*.
Consumed with honey, it destroys old age along with its diseases and even untimely death;
it overcomes even incurable illnesses within seven days—there is nothing equal to this, not even the nectar of the gods.
Castor oil, guñjā, honey, and a ṭaṅka of kaṇa, when rubbed together,
cause the essence derived from *mākṣika* ore to liquefy upon its application.
Then Vimala:
"Vimala is said to be of three kinds: that which begins with gold, that which begins with silver, and the third is the brass-like *vimala*; it is characterized by their respective lusters."
Circular, with well-defined corners, smooth, and provided with a plank;
it removes wind and bile, is aphrodisiac, pure, and an excellent rejuvenative.
The first is said to be for gold-work, the second is considered for silver-work, and the third for medicinal preparations; among these, each preceding one possesses superior qualities.
One who has been purified by bathing in *āṭarūṣa* water becomes stainless; likewise, one purified by bathing in the fresh juice of a citron, or in the juice of *meṣaśṛṅgī*, becomes stainless.
It attains purity like other stainless elements;
it is killed by ten *puṭa* cycles using fragrance, stone, *lakucha*, and sour substances.
Having ground [the substance] with the juices of *saṭaṅka* and *lakuc*, and with the ash of *meṣaśṛṅgī*,
it should be smeared inside the crucible, dried, and then sealed.
Blown by six pairs of kokila-blowing pipes, it becomes stainless and resembles lead;
when combined with that, the mercury releases its essence (sattva), and that mercury shall be an elixir (rasāyana).
Vimala, combined with kaṅkṣī, kāsīsa, ṭaṅkaṇa,
and vajrakanda, should be processed with the juice of the kadali plant using the water of the śigru tree.
When combined with the juice of *mokṣaka* and heated in a sealed crucible (*mūkamūṣā*), the essence falls out resembling the moon and sun; of this there is no doubt.
Having ground that sattva thoroughly and mixed it with mercury,
one should cast it into melted sulphur and digest it until three times the amount of *ālaka* has been assimilated.
One should indeed place the stone possessing five qualities along with sand in a mechanical apparatus, together with a tenth part of silver ash, and likewise with dead vaikrānta.
Having ground everything together into one mass and filtered it through a cloth,
one should carefully place it inside a small jar and fill it to the brim with effort.
Licked with *vyoṣa* and *varā*, combined with *vimalaka* and taken with ghee, it destroys diseases caused by misfortune, fevers, swellings, anemia, urinary disorders, and loss of appetite;

it also cures pain in the bladder, malabsorption syndrome, incomparable colic, consumption, jaundice, all diseases of bile and wind, and—what need for other formulations?—all diseases without exception.
Thus [ends the section on] Vimala.

Now, regarding the mineral ores (*śilādhātu*): the mineral ore is said to be of two kinds—the *rasāyana* type beginning with "cow's urine" (*gomūtra*) and another beginning with "camphor" (*karpūra*). Of these, the first is further divided into two types. (VR 2.109)
Between these two, the one with a living being and the one without a living being, the former is superior in quality;
[as seen in the case of] the snow-capped mountain compared to the feet scorched by the fierce sun in summer.
Mineral ore may be extracted from mountains containing gold, silver, or copper;
that which is born from a mountain containing gold is heavy and resembles a hibiscus flower.
Slightly bitter and very sweet, it is the supreme elixir;
born from a mountain containing silver, it is sweet, pale-white, and heavy.
Śilāja, born from a mountain, destroys diseases of bile and specifically removes anemia;
it is copper-colored within, blue in hue, dense, and heavy.
That which is produced from stone (śilāja), which destroys phlegm and wind, is bitter and hot, and cures the disease of consumption (kṣaya)—
that which, when thrown into fire, takes the shape of a linga and remains smokeless,
and which dissolves in water, is indeed pure śilājatu.
Truly, it pacifies fever, anemia, and swelling; it removes urinary disorders and weak digestion; it effects the reduction of fat and alleviates consumption (yakṣman);

it uproots the disease of colic; it destroys abdominal tumors and splenic enlargement; it cures stomach and cardiac pain and eliminates undigested matter (āma); it destroys all skin diseases—what more can be said? It is beneficial for both the body and for metal.
Whatever qualities reside in mercury, the secondary minerals, the lord of metals, gems, and base metals,
they all dwell within the mineral *śilādhātu*, desiring to conquer old age and death.
Śilājatu is indeed purified when washed with alkaline substances, sour liquids, cow’s urine, and water;
likewise, śilādhātu is purified with milk, and triphalā with the juices of ārkava.
Having placed it in an iron vessel,
one should purify it with great care while it is situated within a sudation apparatus (svedanīyantra), combined with alkaline substances, acids, and guggulu.
Sweated for the duration of one *ghaṭikā*, realgar (*śilādhātu*) becomes purified by means of mica,
sulphur, and *mātuluṅga* juice.
For mineral ore, when encased in a crucible, is indeed killed by eight applications of mountain-ash.

One should consume an equal measure of *vaikrāntaka*—which arises from stone reduced to ash, is peerless, and beautiful—combined with *triphalā*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), and ghee, along with an amount equal to a *valla*.

This is effective for anemia, consumption, loss of digestive fire, urinary disorders, diseases of the seminal root, abdominal tumors, splenic enlargement, massive abdominal dropsy, various types of colic, and disorders of the female reproductive tract. (VR 2.121)
If one practices this for six months according to the procedure for elixirs (*rasāyana*),
one shall be freed from wrinkles and graying hair and live happily for a hundred years.
Having ground the mountain-born [mineral] with the group of liquefiers along with sour liquids,
one should place it inside a crucible, seal it, and heat it intensely with kokila-blowing.
One should extract the essence from the mineral rock, which resembles iron when blown upon by breath;
it is white, has the appearance of sand, and consists of *śilājatu* such as camphor and other substances.
It destroys dysuria, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, jaundice, and anemia;
when combined with the water of cardamom (*elā*), it becomes perfected and attains purity.
The Buddhas have not prescribed its killing or the precipitation of its essence (*sattvapātana*).
Then Sasyaka [said]:
"Having drunk the *hālāhala* poison vomited up by Garuḍa after he had swallowed the nectar,
[I was born] from that poison mixed with nectar upon the mountain named Marakata."
For that which has been vomited up and has become solidified indeed becomes *sasyaka*;
it is highly praised when it possesses the luster of a peacock’s neck and is rich in weight.

Whatever substance is mixed with poison will possess qualities exceeding those of the substance itself; likewise, Hālāhala poison mixed with nectar will possess qualities exceeding those of the nectar.

Mayūratuttha is declared here as a supreme elixir that removes all defects, poisons, heart disease, colic, leprosy, acidity, bile disorders, and constipation; it performs emesis and purgation, destroys toxins, and cures vitiligo.
Sasyaka attains purity when processed with the group of red substances,
sprinkled with the group of oily substances, and [repeated] seven times without being spoiled.
Sasyaka (copper pyrite) that has been well-sweated in a dolāyantra for three praharas is purified as five kharparas when processed in the urine of cows, buffaloes, and goats.
Combined with the juice of *lakucha*, sulphur, and *ṭaṅkaṇa* salt,
and sealed within a crucible, it is killed by means of *kaukkuṭa* cupelings.
One should place the powder of *sasyaka* combined with a quarter-part of *saubhāgya* within *karañja* oil for one day.
One should heat three *kokila* [minerals] placed inside the mouth of a blind crucible;
the resulting essence (*sattva*) will be beautiful, having the appearance of an *indragopa* insect.
Having sealed copper within a crucible using the juice of *nimbū* and *alpaṭaṅka*,
and heating it thoroughly, the *sasyaka* ore releases its essence.
Pure grain, pressed by stones and combined with previously mentioned medicinal substances,
certainly releases the essence through various methods of application.
Having taken this essence, one who consumes the essence of a donkey, the earth, or a nāga,
and touches a seal made from it, shall instantly become a destroyer of the trident-bearer (Śiva).
This mudrā, which produces immediate proof, should be performed to conquer the poison of all moving and unmoving beings that has entered the sight of *bhūtas* and *ḍākinīs*. VRs 2.138.
Likewise, on the northern side of the Himālaya, there is the great tree Aśvakarṇa, which bears the same syllables as those impressed by Rāma’s son Soma.
There, the pain arose and there itself it vanished;
the water from the mudrā, consecrated seven times with this mantra, was drunk.
"This is declared by Bhāluki to be an instant cure for colic;
oil heated over a fire with this mudrā is certainly effective. (VR 2.141)
When applied as a plaster, it violently destroys colic wherever it may arise;
it immediately induces labor in a woman and instantly cures eye diseases.
Now, regarding the *capala* (the volatile mercury):
"The *capala* is of four kinds—white, pale-yellow, reddish, and black;
that which has the luster of gold or the stars is especially capable of binding the mercury. (VR 2.143)
The remaining two middle types are like lac in that they melt quickly, yet they are fruitless;
because it melts in fire like tin, it is celebrated as *capala*.
Copper is considered to be stimulating, softening, unctuous, and beneficial for the body and the blood;
it is an ally to mercury (rasarāja) and is regarded as bitter, hot, and sweet.
Capala is of the luster of crystal, hexagonal, glossy, and heavy;
it destroys the three doṣas, is highly aphrodisiac, and facilitates the binding of mercury.
Indeed, by some, Capala is proclaimed among the great minerals (mahārasas).
The purification of a fickle person is by means of jambīra, karkoṭaka, and ginger, along with repeated contemplations.
Having pulverized a mountain with grains, fermented liquors, and poisons,
one should fashion a ball according to the ritual and likewise cause a fickle person to fall.
Now, regarding *rasaka*: *rasaka* is said to be of two kinds—*durdura* and *kāravellaka*.
That which has leaves is called *durdura*, while that which is leafless is *kāravellaka*. (VRrs 2.149)
When the mercury falls, the first [product] is auspicious; the second is used for medicinal herbs and the like.
This *rasaka* destroys all types of urinary disorders (*meha*) and eliminates phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
Both the *rasa* and the *rasaka*, which destroy eye diseases and consumption, and which color iron and mercury,
were taught by Nāgārjuna.

The two excellent perfected elixirs (siddharasa) are renowned as the supreme agents for transforming both the body and base metals; they are mercury and calamine, by which both are rendered capable of withstanding fire.
There is no doubt that for him, the accomplishment of an iron-like body becomes his servant.
One should cook *rasaka* after stirring it with the extract of bitter *alābu*.
A heated skull-cup, when immersed seven times [in cow's urine], becomes pure, free from defects, and turns yellow in color.
It attains a state of internal purity within the juice of the citron,
or in human urine, or in horse urine, or in buttermilk, or in sour gruel.
A skull-cup that has been thoroughly heated and then immersed [in the liquid] becomes completely purified;
a mineral pigment (rasaka) kept in human urine for a month will certainly be dyed.
Pure copper and mercury, which has the luster of pure silver or gold,
[is processed] with turmeric, the three myrobalans, lac, rock salt, soot, and borax.
Having ground together one part of *sāruṣkara* with sour substances in an iron pan,
one should smear it onto a gourd-shaped crucible (*vṛntākamūṣā*), dry it, and then seal it.
Having placed the crucible over the mouth of the furnace, one should then blow into it;
if, when the crucible is struck, the flame becomes blue or white, [the process is successful].
Then, having seized the crucible with tongs and turned it face downwards,
one should gently tap it against the ground so that the tube does not break.
One should take up the substance that has fallen, which has the luster of tin, and apply it;
in this way, after three or four applications, the entire substance will emerge.
Lead ore (sābhraya), realgar (jatubhū), mica (nāga), orpiment (niśā), soot (dhūma), and borax (jaṭaṅkaṇa),
when placed in a sealed crucible (mūkamūṣā) and heated, release their pure essence (sattva).
Having thoroughly powdered lac, jaggery, *āsuri*, *pathyā*, turmeric, *sarja* resin, and borax,
one should cook it with cow’s milk and clarified butter.
Having enclosed a mouse within the middle of a gourd and shaped it into the form of a pill,
one should repeatedly blow upon it, draw it out, and crush it upon a stone surface.
One should take mercury in the form of a fish, which is pleasing to the mind;
or else, one should bury a vessel containing water within the interior of a crucible.
One should place a perforated crucible over its mouth and an inverted one over that;
having cast the fire within the crucible, one should heat it firmly.
One should take the essence fallen into the water of the vessel and combine it;
having indeed cast that essence together with talaka into a shallow pan, [one should proceed].
One should crush it with an iron rod until it certainly becomes ash;
one should then mix that ash with an equal amount of dead iron (mṛtakānta).

Eight *guñjā*s of this powder, combined with a decoction of *triphalā* and placed in a vessel of magnetic stone (*kāntapātra*) overnight, should be used as a counter-incantation (*prativāpaka*) over sesame seeds.
When practiced regularly, it certainly and swiftly destroys even diabetes mellitus.
It cures bile disorders, wasting, jaundice, edema, abdominal tumors,
as well as uterine tumors in women, menorrhagia, and somaroga.
It cures all gynecological diseases without exception, as well as irregular fevers,
menstrual pain in women, cough, asthma, and hiccups.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Eightfold Mercury, Purification, and Other Processes," in the *Rasaratnasamuccaya* composed by Ācārya Vāgbhaṭa, son of the illustrious Vaidyapati Siṃhagupta.
Now begins the third chapter:
[Next, the secondary minerals and the common minerals]. Now, regarding sulfur (gandhaka):
Sulphur, realgar, iron pyrite, orpiment, talc, mica,
antimony, and kaṅkuṣṭha— these are the eight secondary minerals (uparasas) used in the processing of mercury.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, tell me that secret majesty of Gandhaka.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, in former times, on the shore of the Ocean of Milk— on the delightful White Island (Śvetadvīpa), adorned with all kinds of jewels and consisting of every object of desire.
And by the foremost women of the Vidyādharas and others,
as well as by the excellent wives of the Siddhas and by hosts of Apsarases, [the yogins were honored].
He was entertained by charming celestial damsels who played delightful games,
and by captivating songs, diverse dances, and various kinds of musical instruments.
As she was thus sporting, her flowing menses appeared;
that menses, O lady of beautiful hips, was exceedingly fragrant and most enchanting.
Due to the excessive abundance of dust, your garment turned red;
having bathed well there in the Ocean of Milk, you cast that garment aside.
Surrounded by celestial nymphs, you have returned to Kailāsa;
meanwhile, that garment of dust has been carried into the midst of the ocean by its waves.
Thus, O blessed lady, your blood entered the Ocean of Milk;
and during the churning of the milk-ocean, it emerged together with the nectar of immortality.
Delighting all those Danavas at all times with his own fragrance, he was then addressed by the hosts of gods: "Let him be named Gandhaka."
"May this [process] serve for the binding and the digestion of mercury;
may all those qualities that have been proclaimed for pārada be present here as well. (VRṣ 3.10)
Thus was it spoken of old by the delighted hosts of gods, O Queen of the Suras;
therefore, this substance is renowned on the surface of the earth by the name Gandhaka.
And that [flower], O Goddess, is also of three kinds: the best is like the beak of a parrot; the middling is yellow in color; and the lowest, O Beloved, is white in color.
In another treatise, sulphur is known to be of four kinds according to its colors, beginning with white;
here, the white variety is called khaṭikā, used for plastering and for the killing of metals.
Likewise, that which is pure and possesses a yellow color would be like a parrot's wing; it alone is the best for the purpose of alchemical elixirs.
And the red variety called *śukatuṇḍa* is excellent for the practice of alchemy;
it is difficult to find in black color, and it destroys old age and death.

The mineral Gandhāśman is considered an excellent rejuvenative (rasāyana), very sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka), pungent, and hot; it destroys itching, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), and ringworm (dadrū); it kindles the digestive fire, acts as a digestive (pācana), releases undigested matter (āma), and is drying; it is an antidote to poison, bestows the potency of mercury (sūtendra), and likewise destroys worms; it is of truthful nature and overcomes mercury. (VR 3.16)
It was formerly resorted to by Balarāma for the sake of obtaining great strength.
As he was pulling Vāsuki, the fat, rich with the scent of sulfur, melted by the flame from his mouth and issued forth from every part of his body.
Having attained the state of being a fragrant substance (*gandhakatva*), it became known as "poisonous fragrance" (*saviṣagandha*).
Therefore, this exceedingly captivating fragrant substance is called *balivasā*.
Sulfur that has been steamed in milk for the duration of one ghaṭī and washed with water,
when melted in cow’s clarified butter and strained through a cloth, attains purity.
Thus purified, this [consciousness] abandons its stone-like nature,
its form of husks within clarified butter, and even its own state of being a solid mass.
Thus, for indeed, pure sulphur does not undergo corruption through unwholesome [substances];
otherwise, due to unwholesomeness, it would destroy [the patient], just like the Hālāhala poison when drunk.
Sulfur, when melted and cast into the juice of *bhṛṅga*, becomes purified;
sulfur is completely purified when it has been divided seven times by those juices.
Having poured milk into a pot and tied a cloth over its mouth,
one should place powdered sulphur, which has the consistency of sand, into it.
One should cover the sulphur with a wide and long earthen pan;
one should then ignite it from above the pan using wood-chips and stones.
When the sulphur falls into the milk, having melted, it becomes completely purified.
Thus, when purified and mixed with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), clarified butter, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and honey, and consumed in a dose of one *śāṇa*,
it makes the pair of eyes equal to those of a vulture and brings about a long life free from disease.
Having finely powdered sulphur combined with a one-sixteenth part of the three pungents (vyoṣa),
one should scatter it over a cloth measuring one cubit (aratni) in length and wrap it up.
Then, having wrapped it with thread, one should immerse it in oil for a watch;
holding it with tongs, one should ignite the wick in the middle.
The liquefied fragrance should be dropped drop by drop into a glass vessel;
one should then place three drops of that liquid upon a betel leaf.
One should grind the pure lord of mercury (sūtendra), measured by a *valla*, together with that liquefied substance (*druti*) and the leaf;
then, with one's finger, one should consume that liquefaction and the mercury.
It produces intense digestion, cures consumption, anemia, and wasting;
it also overcomes cough, dyspnea, colic pain, and even the most difficult-to-subdue disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
Pure sulphur, melted in an iron vessel smeared with ghee, quickly destroys undigested matter (āma) and brings about lightness.
One should consume two niṣkas of this, cast from a ladle smeared with ghee;
it destroys diseases such as consumption, and especially leprosy.
One engaged in yoga must indeed avoid alkaline substances, acids, oils, fermented gruel, burning foods, and pulses while practicing pure sulfur.
Gandhaka mixed with an equal amount of marica, combined with six times the quantity of triphalā,
and rubbed with the root of śamyāka, when drunk, destroys all types of kuṣṭha.
One should apply a paste ground in its root-water to the body every day;
this is a practice whose efficacy is proven and which possesses great potency in all circumstances.
The illustrious Somadeva has correctly described here [the following]:
having ground two niṣkas of fragrant substance and combined it with oil...
Then, having anointed his entire body with the water of the apāmārga plant mixed with oil and black pepper, he should thereafter remain steadfast in dharma.
In the third watch of the day, he should indeed eat rice with buttermilk;
likewise, having risen early in the morning, he should attend to the sacred fire at night.
Having smeared himself with buffalo dung, he should bathe with cold water;
then, having anointed his body with ghee, he should bathe with pleasantly warm water.
By this sequential method, even that itch and scabies which has been difficult to conquer and long-standing will certainly perish with extreme rapidity. (VRs 3.41)
A hundred applications of perfumes have not been proclaimed here by King Somadeva, for fear of excessive prolixity in this work.
Alternatively, one should coat a cloth seven times with the milks of the arka and snuhī plants;
then, having ground sulphur with fresh butter, one should smear the cloth thickly with it.
One should place that wick, smeared with ghee, burning at the bite-mark with its tip facing downward;
the oil that falls into the vessel below should be collected and employed in medicinal formulations.
Pure *gandha* removes diseases such as leprosy, death, and old age;
it generates fire, is greatly heating, and increases virility.
Now, regarding *gaurika*:
there is one, stone-gairika, and a second, gold-gairika.
Stone-gairika is said to be hard and copper-colored.
Gold ochre (svarṇagairika) is extremely red, unctuous, and smooth;
it is sweet, unctuous, cooling, beneficial for the eyes, astringent, and subdues blood-bile (raktapitta).
Gold ochre (svarṇagairika) destroys hiccup, vomiting, and poison, and it is blood-purifying;
the other, stone ochre (pāṣāṇagairika), is slightly inferior to the former in its qualities.
Red ochre, when saturated with cow's milk, attains purity;
for red ochre is said by Nandin to be of the nature of *sattva*.
Some have said that the sattva falls from red ochre moistened with alkaline acid;
it attends upon the lord of mercury (sūtendra) and becomes unified, possessing even greater qualities.
Now, regarding *kāsīsa*:
*Kāsīsa* is of two kinds—one is like sand and the like, and the other is preceded by flowers;
it resembles the smoke of alkaline, sour, and *agaru* incense, possesses a hot potency (*uṣṇavīrya*), and destroys poison.
Sandalwood, saffron, and green vitriol destroy leucoderma and dye the hair.

Realgar (kāsīsa), along with flowers and other ingredients, is highly praised; when heated, it is intensely astringent and slightly sour, extremely beneficial for the eyes, a destroyer of diseases caused by poison, wind, and phlegm, a healer of wounds, a remover of vitiligo and consumption, and a hair-dye.
Kāsīsa becomes pure when moistened once with the water of bees;
one may extract its essence just as one extracts the essence from *tuvarī*.
Kāsīsa attains purity through bile, and [the impurity of] women through menstrual blood.
Equal parts of *kāsīsa* killed by mercury (*balinā*) and *kāsīsa* killed by mercury (*krānta-kāsīsa-mārita*) should be combined with an equal amount of *triphalā* and *vella*.
Taken at dawn in a dose of one śāṇa, saturated with an unequal portion of ghee and honey,
it swiftly destroys vitiligo, anemia, and consumption.
When consumed for the duration of a year according to the procedure for elixirs (rasāyana), it cures abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, colic, and especially diseases of the bowels.
The consumption of *āma* is excellent for kindling a weak digestive fire;
it certainly destroys gray hair along with wrinkles.
Now, as for *tuvarī*:
that which is produced in Saurāṣṭra is considered *tuvarī*;
that which adheres to clothes and binds the dye is *mañjiṣṭhā*.
And the second is proclaimed as Phaṭakīphullikā;
it is slightly yellow, heavy, and unctuous, and this yellow variety destroys poison.
It removes wounds and leprosy, and specifically destroys all types of skin diseases.
Light, white in color, and glossy, it is considered another variety known as *sāmlā*;
that which is called *phullatuvarī* turns copper into iron when applied as a paste.
It is astringent, bitter, sour, and pungent; it is beneficial for the hair, heals wounds, and destroys poison.
It removes vitiligo, is good for the eyes, provides relief from the three *doṣas*, and acts as a solvent for mercury.
Having thrown *tuvarī* into sour gruel (*kāñjika*), it attains purification after three days;
when rubbed with alkaline substances and acids and then smelted, it certainly releases its essence (*sattva*).
Then, one should saturate a hundred pieces of *saurāṣṭra* with cow-bile;
having blown upon them, one should extract the essence (*sattva*), which is an exceedingly secret method of transference (*krāmaṇa*).
Now, regarding *tālaka*: realgar (*haritāla*) is said to be of two kinds—the first is known as *pratyādya* and the other as *piṇḍa*.
That which is golden-colored, heavy, unctuous, capable of being made into thin leaves, and radiant is the *pratyādya*.

That which has leaf-like scales is called *patratālaka*; that with many scales is an elixir (*rasāyana*). That which is scaleless and resembles a solid mass (*piṇḍa*) is of little essence, heavy, and it destroys female menses; such is *piṇḍatālaka*, which possesses few qualities.

Haritāla is said to destroy phlegm, blood, poison, wind, and spirits; it is exclusively effective against women who steal flowers, is unctuous, hot, pungent, digestive, and a remover of skin diseases (kuṣṭha).
It becomes purified by means of the dolāyantra (swinging apparatus) when soaked in the juice of ash-gourd, or in water mixed with sesame-alkali,
or in water combined with a powder.
Impure *tāla* destroys life, increases phlegm, wind, and urinary disorders, and causes eruptions, body sores, and contractions of the limbs; therefore, one should purify it.
Having reduced the talaka to fine particles and adding a tenth part of ṭaṅkaṇa,
it should be washed with juices from jambīra fruits and then washed with kāñjika.
Having tied it in a fourfold cloth, one should cook it in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra) for a day.
Or, tālaka may attain purification by being sweated for a day in the juice of kūṣmāṇḍa with powdered *āranāla*, or with the waters of *śālmalī*.
Having ground the mineral cinnabar (tālaka) three times in a thick decoction of *brahmamūla* that is like honey, it should then be processed in buffalo urine.
Having sealed the crucible with ten stones, one should then grind it;
thus it should be cooked twelve times, and once purified, it may be employed in medicinal formulations.
Having placed it in a pot along with the auspicious milk of a buffalo saturated with *kuṣṭha* decoction, clarified butter, and honey,
one should cook it over a fire using a vessel provided with a small hole.
Having properly sealed it, one should ignite the fire, increasing it gradually,
for the duration of one watch (three hours), having covered the opening with cow-dung.
At the end of the watch, having opened the aperture and seeing pale smoke,
one should remove the cold vessel, extract the essence, and take it away.
There are indeed millions of varieties of all stone-beings;
however, fearing excessive prolixity, I have certainly not written of them here.
One should grind palālaka with the milks of the sun (goat's milk) for one day;
having cast it into *ṣoḍaśikā* oils and mixed them together, one should then cook it.
And in an unobstructed place, one should certainly collect a white being that has been lying beneath for seven watches, its own body parts cooled.
Then, having diligently ground together the gallstone of a goat and that of a young calf, along with mercury and a pair of *duvasat* [sulphur] salts;
One should place it, combined with the group of fluxing agents, into a glass crucible;
having smeared it three times with clay and dried it thoroughly in the hot sun.
Then, having inserted that half-portion and the small jar into the opening of the crucible,
one should kindle the fire for a period of twelve hours.
One should collect the cool, pure essence situated at the throat of the *kupī* plant,
measuring half a *pala*, having tied it in a firm white cloth.
Having carefully smeared it with *balī* and dried it three times,
one should throw a small cloth-pouch of *tālaka* into the molten copper containing the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
One should quickly cover it with ash and encase it in white copper; from this, one should extract the soft essence, as prescribed for the elixir of mercury.
Now, regarding realgar (manaḥśilā): realgar is said to be of three kinds—Śyāmāṅgī, Kaṇavīrakā, and that called Khaṇḍā;
its nature is described here after having been analyzed.
Śyāmā, Raktā, and Gaurā are considered to be heavy; Śyāmikā is also regarded as such.
Tejasvinī is devoid of whiteness, while Kaṇavīrakā has a coppery luster.
With her limbs exceedingly red and powdered, possessing her full weight and preceded by the [first] half-verse,
she is proclaimed as "Abounding in Beings" (Bhūrisattvā), excellent due to the qualities mentioned subsequently.
Realgar is the foremost of all rejuvenative elixirs; it is bitter, pungent, and hot, and it destroys phlegm and wind.
Being of the nature of consciousness (*sattva*), it removes possession by spirits, poisons, sluggish digestion, itching, cough, and consumption.
If impure, the stone (śilā) causes urinary calculi and dysuria;
if purified, it removes all diseases, though it may cause weak digestion and constipation.
Realgar is purified by being infused seven times with water from the leaves of the Agastya plant,
or else with the juices of ginger.
One should cook the mineral (śilā) for one hour each in the juices of *jayantī*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, red [pigment], and *agastya*,
and for one hour each in goat's urine;
then one should wash it with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*) and employ it in all diseases.

When manahśilā is enclosed within a crucible together with its eighth part of dross (kiṭṭa), along with jaggery, guggulu, and clarified butter, and is strongly heated by blowing, it releases its essence (sattva).
Having ground together *bhūnāga*, *dhauta*, *saubhāgya*, and *madana*,
one should prepare a crucible with water from the leaves of *kāravallī* and place [the mixture] therein.
Immediately thereafter, one should blow [into the mouth] a stone ground with alkaline acid;
indeed, by blowing [it] for about the duration of two *kokila* birds, it causes that [creature] to abandon its life-force.
Now, regarding collyriums: sauvīra collyrium is proclaimed, and after that, rasāñjana;
then there is srotoñjana, and also puṣpāñjana.
Now, their specific characteristics are described here: blue antimony (nīlāñjana) is smoky-colored sauvīrāñjana; it is cooling and removes blood-bile disorders.
Rasāñjana, which has a yellowish luster, destroys poison, hiccup, and eye diseases; it cleanses and heals wounds and removes diseases of the mouth.
Srotoñjana removes dyspnea and hiccups, improves the complexion, and destroys wind, bile, and blood disorders;
it is cooling, unctuous, astringent, sweet, and scraping.
Indeed, *netrī* cures hiccups, poisoning, vomiting, diseases of phlegm, bile, and blood.
White *puṣpāñjana* is unctuous and cooling; it cures all eye diseases, overcomes even most difficult-to-restrain hiccups, and removes poison, fever, and other ailments.
Blue antimony is heavy, unctuous, beneficial for the eyes, and removes the three *doṣas*;
it is an elixir (*rasāyana*), destroys gold, and makes iron malleable.
Collyriums are purified by the natural juices of *bhṛṅgarāja*;
one should collect the essence of realgar and the essence of *sattvavajra* for the purpose of collyriums.

A wise person should recognize *srotoja* (antimony) by its appearance: it has the shape of an anthill's summit, possesses the luster of a blue lotus when broken, and has the hue of white chalk when rubbed.
When repeatedly saturated with cow dung, liquid and urine, as well as ghee, honey, and fat,
that [mercury] quickly binds the essence of mercury (sūtaka).
Through the application of *sūryāvarta* and other methods, *rasāñjana* attains purity;
likewise, the essence should be extracted from *srotoñjana* just as it is from *rājāvartaka*.
Now, regarding kaṅkuṣṭha:
Kaṅkuṣṭha is produced on the peaks at the foot of the Himavat mountains;
there, one type is indeed called nālikā, while the other is considered to be reṇuka.
Kaṅkuṣṭha that is yellowish-lustrous, heavy, and unctuous is the best of the first type;
however, that which is dark-yellow, light, and devoid of essence is indeed undesirable as it is merely *reṇuka*.
Some say that the dung of a newborn elephant,
appearing dark yellowish-green, is described as a purgative known as *kaṅkuṣṭha*.
They say that *kaṅkuṣṭha*, which has the appearance of white or yellow and is known as "the life-force of the few," is an extremely potent purgative.

Among metallic substances (rasas), kaṅkuṣṭha is the best elixir (rasāyana); it is devoid of essence, possesses many transformative properties, is bitter and pungent, hot in potency, and a powerful purgative.
It removes pain from wounds, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and ailments of the rectum.
The sun-turning plant, the banana, the barren luffa, the kośātakī, the suradālī, the drumstick tree, the vajrakanda, the niraṅkaṇā, and the kākamācī.

When repeatedly treated with salt, alkali, and sour substances using a single essence of these, the primary and secondary minerals (rasoparasa) become purified; when smelted, they release their essences (sattva).
Kaṅkuṣṭha attains purification by being infused three times with ginger-water;
no extraction of its essence (sattva) is prescribed, because it is indeed composed of that essence.
One should consume this with a dose the size of a barley grain along with binding substances for the purpose of purgation;
having induced purging in a mere moment, it destroys the accumulation of undigested matter (āmavipāka).
If consumed together with betel leaves, it causes purging and may destroy life.
A person should drink, repeatedly, equal parts of a decoction of *barburī* root, cumin, *saubhāgyaka*,
and *kaṅkuṣṭha* for the destruction of poison.
Thus are the minor metallic salts (uparasas).
Now, the common minerals (sādhāraṇarasas): kampilla, capala, gaurīpāṣāṇa, and navasāraka.
Kaparda, vahnijāra, girisindūra, and hiṅgula; // VRrs_3.120 //
Modāraśṛṅga and the others—these eight are known as the common rasas;
they are declared by the masters headed by Nāgārjuna to be the means for accomplishing the attainment of rasa.
Now, regarding *kampilla*:
resembling the powder of bricks, rich in luster, and highly purgative;
produced in the region of Saurāṣṭra, it is indeed known as *kampillaka*.

Kampillaka destroys bile-born ulcers, flatulence, and constipation; it is the enemy of phlegm-born abdominal diseases, worms, and tumors; it removes root-diseases, scrotal swellings, fever, and colic; and it is a purgative that dispels all maladies.
Now, regarding the *gaurīpāṣāṇa*: the *gaurīpāṣāṇaka* is known to be of three types—yellow, *vikaṭa*, and *hatacūrṇaka*; it may also resemble crystal, a conch shell, or turmeric. (VR 3.124)
One should place each preceding substance, superior in its qualities, inside a *kāravallī* fruit;
by steaming it within a crucible (*haṇḍikā*), the mouse-mercury becomes purified.
One should cause the being to grasp [the essence] like a palm fruit; one should employ that which is pure and bright.
It binds the mercury, is unctuous, destroys the defects, and produces the potency of the mercury.
Now, regarding *navasāra*:
this alkali (*kṣāra*) produced when the wood of the *karīra* and *pīlu* trees is being burned is *navasāra*, also known by the name *cūlikālavaṇa*.
The white, light salt produced by burning bricks is called *navasāra* and is also known as *cūlikālavaṇa*. It facilitates the digestion of mercury,
liquefies metals, and stimulates the digestive fire.

Cūlikā-lavaṇa is considered to destroy abdominal tumors (gulma), splenic disorders, and dryness of the mouth; it digests meat and other foods just consumed, and it is known as viḍa-salt, which alleviates the three doṣas.
Now, regarding the cowries:
a yellowish, knotted, long, and oval shell on its back is designated by physicians of mercury as *varāṭikā*; it is known by the names *cara* and *acara*.
The best [quality] is said to weigh one and a half niṣkas; the middling, one niṣka;
and the lowest, three-quarters of a niṣka.

It cures colic caused by morbid transformation and other disorders, destroys malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) and consumption (kṣaya), is pungent and hot, stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and removes wind and phlegm.
It is prescribed for the digestion of mercury by the alchemists and is highly recommended among the substances used as *biḍa*.
But other types of cowries are heavy and increase phlegm and bile;
cowries attain purification after being soaked in fermented rice-water (kāñjika) for one watch (yāma).
Now, regarding *agnijāra*:
the placenta of the fire-crocodile was cast out by the ocean;
having dried up under the heat of the sun, it is known as *agnijāra*.
Agnijāra destroys the three doṣas and cures vāta disorders such as dhanurvāta;
it increases the potency and strength of rasa, and acts as a digestive stimulant and a digestant.
Since it is purified by the alkaline water of the sea, no further purification is required for it.
Now, regarding *girisindūra*:
it is a liquid substance situated within small stones found on great mountains;
when dried, it is designated by the name *girisindūra*.
Girisindūra is said to pacify the three humors (tridoṣa), act as a purgative, be the foremost binder of mercury, strengthen the body and iron, and benefit the eyes.
Now, regarding cinnabar (hiṅgula): Cinnabar is called *śukatuṇḍa*, and another is *haṃsapāka*.
Of these, the first has few qualities; it is designated as *carmāra*.
That which is white with the luster of coral is called haṃsapāka;
it destroys all defects, stimulates digestion, and is an excellent elixir.
It removes all diseases, is aphrodisiac, and is highly praised for the process of digestion (*jāraṇā*); the mercury extracted from this possesses qualities equal to that of digested sulfur.
Having been dried seven times with the juice of fresh ginger or with the water of *lakuca*,
and then infused, it indeed becomes free from defects.

What is there to wonder at in this? Darada, when well-processed with goat's milk and repeatedly with the group of sour substances, likewise makes gold—when heated many times by intense heat—possess the very luster of excellent saffron.
When cinnabar (darada) is precipitated in a *pātanāyantra* and placed in a water-receptacle, its essence—which resembles mercury—will precipitate;
of this there is no doubt.
Now, regarding *mṛddāraśṛṅgaka*: it is multi-faceted and yellow in color, found in the region of Gurjara;
*mṛddāraśṛṅgaka* is that which is produced on the slopes of Mount Arbuda.
Lead-sattva is heavy, pacifies phlegm, removes diseases of men,
is excellent for binding mercury, and is supreme for blackening the hair.
All common medicinal substances, when processed for three nights with the juice of *mātuluṅga* and fresh ginger and then dried, become free from defects.
Whatever beings there may be, they are purified without exception;
blown by the wind of purification, they come together with one another.
Thus ends [the description of] Karavālabhairava.
Now, regarding Rājāvarta:
Rājāvarta has a luster mixed with slight redness and deep blue.
That which is heavy and smooth is the best; any other is considered middling.
Rājāvarta removes urinary disorders, consumption, skin diseases, anemia, phlegm, and wind;
it is digestive, carminative, aphrodisiac, and an elixir.
Indeed, minerals such as rājāvarta and others are purified after being steamed two or three times with lime juice mixed with cow urine and salt.
One should purify rājāvarta with the fresh juices of śirīṣa flowers.
Rājāvarta, powdered and combined with the fragrance of *luṅga* juice,
becomes "dead" (calcined) after being subjected to *puṭapāka* seven times.
One should cook the powder of rājāvarta mixed with kunaṭī and ghee,
together with buffalo milk, in an iron vessel.
One should cause [the substance] to be assimilated by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with auspicious ingredients;
when blown upon with charcoal from the khadira tree, it releases a beautiful essence (sattva).
By this sequential yoga, the red ochre becomes stainless;
gradually, the yellow and the red essence fall down beautifully.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification and Other Processes of the Subordinate Minerals and Common Metals," in the *Rasaratnasamuccaya* composed by Ācārya Vāgbhaṭa, son of the venerable Vaidyapati Siṃhagupta.
Now begins the fourth chapter. [Now, the jewels:
Now, the gems—
Furthermore, the gems that serve as the binding agents for the mercury should be known;
they are vaikrānta, sūryakānta, diamond, pearl, and maṇi.
Likewise, the moonstone, and rājāvarta as the seventh;
and garuḍodgāraka—these are to be known as the gems.
Topaz, sapphire,
ruby, coral, beryl, and likewise lapis lazuli— these are considered the gems;
they should be collected with great care for the purpose of binding mercury.
The ruby known as padmarāga, the sapphire known as indranīla, the excellent emerald, the topaz, and that which is called diamond— these are remembered as the five supreme jewels.
Garnet, pearl, coral, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, agate,
and cat’s-eye are, in order, the gems of the nine planets.

For the sake of attaining desired success, one should wear as amulets, in their respective order, the planets' friendly stones: kuruvinda, coral, pearl, emerald, diamond, sapphire, hessonite, and cat's-eye.
For the sake of success, well-born gems are said to be easily protected when used for alchemy, elixirs, giving, wearing, or the worship of deities.
The first is the ruby known as *padmarāga*, and the second is the *nīlagandhi*;
it has the luster of a lotus petal, is transparent, glossy, large, and radiant.
A body that is rounded, long, and symmetrical is said to be the most excellent ruby.
That excellent ruby, produced from the waters of the Gaṅgā, possesses a dark-blue hue with a reddish glow within;
it is as superior as a prime ruby and has the fragrance of blue lotuses.
A ruby is defective in eight ways when it is possessed of flaws, hardness, impurity, roughness, lack of clarity, flatness, lightness, and crookedness.
Rubies stimulate digestion, act as an aphrodisiac, and alleviate disorders caused by phlegm, wind, and wasting;
they destroy the influence of spirits and *vetālas*, ward off sin, and eliminate diseases born of past actions.
Now, regarding pearls:
"Gleaming, white, light, glossy, radiant, pure, large, renowned for its water-like luster, and round—such a pearl is auspicious in nine ways. (VR 4.13)

Pearl is light, cooling, and sweet; it bestows luster, improves vision and digestive fire, neutralizes poison, and acts as a purgative. It provides virility, and the pearl-oyster from which it originates quickly and certainly cures disorders of digestion. Thus ends the section on pearls. (VR 4.14)
One should reject pearls that are rough-textured, waterless (lacking luster), dark-brown, copper-colored, resembling salt,
half-white, misshapen, or knotted.
Pearl is considered to destroy phlegm, bile, and wasting; it cures cough, dyspnea, and weak digestion; it is nourishing, aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of burning sensations.
Now, regarding coral: Coral that has the luster of a ripe bimba fruit, which is round, long, and straight,
glossy, free of blemishes, and thick, is auspicious for seven days.
Pale, greyish, fine, scarred, veined with large sinews, weightless, and copper-colored— coral is considered undesirable in these eight ways.

Coral (vidruma) destroys consumption, bile, blood disorders, and cough; it stimulates digestion, promotes the digestion of food, and is light. It pacifies poisons and malevolent spirits, and cures eye diseases.
Now, regarding the Tārkṣya stone:
"The body of the Tārkṣya is considered to possess seven qualities: it is greenish-yellow in color, heavy, glossy, emitting a mass of shimmering rays, auspicious, smooth, and radiant. (VR 4.20)
Tawny, rough, blue, pale, or black; light, flat-nosed, deformed, or dark and coarse—such a *tārkṣya* horse is not recommended.
It cures fever, vomiting, poisoning, dyspnea, derangement of the humors (saṃnipāta), and weak digestion;
it destroys hemorrhoids, anemia, and edema; it is named after Tārkṣya and increases one’s vital energy (ojas).
Now, regarding topaz:
Topaz is heavy, clear, glossy, large, even, soft, resembling the Karṇikāra flower, smooth, and auspicious; it is of eight kinds. (VR 4.23)
One should reject a topaz that is lusterless, rough, dry, yellowish, dark, unevenly raised and depressed, brownish-red, tawny, or pale.
Topaz (puṣparāga) removes poison, vomiting, phlegm, wind, and sluggish digestion;
it pacifies burning sensations, skin diseases, and blood disorders, and is digestive, carminative, and light.
Now, regarding the *vajra*:
the *vajra* is said to be of three kinds—male, female, and neuter.
Among these, each preceding one is superior in this world in terms of its taste, potency, and post-digestive effect.
That which is eight-sided, or has eight facets, six corners, and is exceedingly brilliant—
shining like a rainbow in the clouds— is called the male vajra.
That very [vajra] which is flat in shape is the female vajra; it is round and elongated.
The male is round with a blunt cornered tip and is somewhat heavy. The neuter is slightly heavy.

The female, male, or neuter *vajra* should be joined with the female, male, or neuter [partner] respectively; otherwise, through inversion, it yields no fruit, nor is there any result whatsoever without the male *vajra*.
