Each of these is fourfold according to the distinction of colors such as white and so forth—
namely Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra— bestowing the specific fruits corresponding to each respective color.
"For even that which possesses the most excellent color yields the fruit of an inferior color;
this principle was declared by Bhairava regarding all things whatsoever."

This diamond (vajra) bestows longevity, instantly grants excellent qualities, is aphrodisiac, pacifies the three humors, destroys all diseases, effects the binding and killing of mercury (sūtendra), acts as a digestive stimulant, conquers death, and is indeed like nectar. (VRṢ 4.32)
Whiteness, fear (streaks), spots, lines, and the presence of water within—
these five defects are considered common to all gems.
Defects arising from the soil or water do not affect those gems;
they have been steamed in a decoction of *kulattha* or boiled in a decoction of *kodrava*.
A vajra that has been sweated for the duration of one watch (three hours) certainly becomes pure;
a vajra purified four times with the blood of a bedbug [attains purity].
Having kneaded it with the flesh of fragrant mice made into balls,
one should wrap it and then roast it thirty times using the "boar" (varāha) type of puṭa-furnace.
Having blown [the bellows] repeatedly a hundred times, one should cast it into a decoction of *kulattha* beans;
others have stated that this procedural sequence must be performed a hundred times.
Having placed a diamond into a crucible smeared with mica ground with the juice of *lakucha* mixed with a decoction of horse gram (*kulattha*), and having sealed it, [one should proceed].
One should properly roast it eight times with dried wild lotuses;
then, having blown upon it a hundred times, when it is cast into pure mercury,
the diamond is certainly killed and becomes ash that flows like water.
The truthful commander of the Soma army, who was fond of the taste [of battle] and possessed of visible proof, spoke this slaying of Vajra.
It has been smeared with the blood of a bedbug and dried seven times.
Placed in an iron vessel filled with the juice of *kāsamarda* and heated seven times, it indeed becomes "vajra-ash."
This sequence was proclaimed by the lord of sages, Brahmajyotis;
it was extracted from the bulbous root of the blue light-creeper and dried in the heat of the sun.
Just as karma is reduced to ashes by the fire of gnosis, so too does the vajra become ash through the earth,
the serpents, and the juice produced from the fruit of passion.
Having smeared it with prepared *kalka*, one should roast it twenty times;
it will become excellent *vajra*-powder, which should be employed in mercury and other substances.
Then, having powdered that vajra and combined it with a small amount of borax,
it will certainly be processed twenty times with the essence of *kharabhūnāga*.
When blown [into a crucible] together with an equal amount of gold, it is to be employed in the elixirs (*rasa*) and other preparations.
Having thoroughly ground it with a threefold liquid and formed it into pills,
when placed in the mouth, it quickly binds loose teeth.

Vajrabhasma (diamond ash) measuring one-thirtieth part, gold one-sixteenth part, silver eight times that, excellent white mercury one-eleventh part, abhraka (mica) eleven parts, tāpyaka (calamine) indeed one-fourth part, vaikrāntaka eight times that, and ṣāḍguṇya six times that; this elixir, when combined with the aforementioned juices, is proclaimed for the attainment of the sixfold qualities.
Now, regarding blue [gems]:
there is the *jalanīla* and the *indranīla*, and of these two, the latter is superior.
That which possesses a blue luster infused with whiteness and is light is the *jalanīla*.
It possesses a dark-blue luster within its blackness, a brilliant hue like Indra’s sapphire.
Uniform in luster, heavy, glossy, transparent, and compact in form,
with a soft core and a shimmering light within— it is the supreme blue gem of sevenfold quality.
It is of seven kinds: soft, rough, weightless, smelling of blood, flat-looking, fine-textured, and water-blue.
Blue [sulfur] is said to cure dyspnea and cough, to be aphrodisiac, to destroy the three doṣas, and to be a great stimulant of digestion; it also destroys irregular fevers, hemorrhoids, and sins.
Now, regarding gomeda:
because it possesses a color similar to cow-dung (gomaya), the gem is called gomeda.
It has the luster of very clear cow's urine; it is transparent, glossy, even, and heavy.
Gomedaka is auspicious when it is free of flaws, smooth, and lustrous; thus it is of eight types.
Lusterless, light, rough-limbed, flattened, covered with veils, devoid of brilliance, and resembling yellow glass— such a *gomeda* stone does not bring auspiciousness.
Gomedaka destroys phlegm and bile, cures consumption and anemia,
stimulates digestion, promotes digestion, improves the appetite, is beneficial for the skin, and awakens the intellect.
Now, regarding lapis lazuli (vaidūrya):
Lapis lazuli is said to be auspicious when it has a dark-blue and white luster, is even, transparent, heavy, and clear, and is encased within a shimmering, beautiful upper garment.
Vaidūrya that is dark, with a luster like water, flat, light, and rough,
and which has a red interior or upper surface, is not at all praised.
Vaidūrya destroys blood-bile (raktapitta), increases wisdom, longevity, and strength;
it cures diseases dominated by pitta, stimulates digestion, and facilitates the elimination of waste.
Now, the purification of gems:
a ruby is purified by sour gruel, a pearl likewise by jayantī;
coral by the group of alkaline substances, and emerald by cow’s milk.
One should stabilize a topaz with *kulattha* bean decoctions wrapped in leaves;
a diamond with *tandulīya* water; and a sapphire with indigo juice.
And one should cleanse *gomeda* with *rocanā*, and *vaidūrya* with the waters of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

Now, the procedure for the ash of gems (ratnabhasmakrama): Gems other than diamond (vajra) are indeed killed by eight layers [of heating] using realgar, sulphur, and talc ground together with the juice of *lakucha*.
Asafoetida, the five salts, the three alkaline substances,
meat broth, sour sorrel, and likewise table salt.
The large ripe kumbhī fruit, as well as the auspicious jvālāmukhī,
dravantī, rudantī, payasyā, and citramūlaka.
Then, having diligently ground together the milk of the *snuhī* plant and that of the *arka* plant,
one should form a ball and subsequently place [the mercury] into its center.
Having fashioned that ball from birch bark using excellent, high-quality, and auspicious gems of pure origin, one should carefully wrap it with thread.
Then, having wrapped it again with cloth and placed it in a swinging apparatus (dolāyantra) inside the belly of a jar completely filled with a fermenting mixture containing all types of acids;
One should cause it to sweat for three days and nights with a fierce fire;
then, having extracted it from there and washed it, one should take the liquid essence produced from the jewels.
Equal in luster to a gem, light, beneficial for the body and the blood, and auspicious;
pearl powder, having been rubbed with cane-juice (*vetasāmla*) for seven days, [is used].
One should place it in the center of a citron and bury it within a heap of grain;
after seven days, having extracted it and placed it in a crucible, liquefaction occurs.
Having placed it within a *vajravallī* vessel, one should block the *vajra*;
once it has been heated while contained in a sour vessel, it will attain the state of liquefaction after seven days.
Now, regarding vaikrānta:
white-colored vaikrānta, when saturated with amlavetasa for seven days, undoubtedly melts in a hot desert sun.
One should take the fresh juice of the *ketakī*, rock salt, and *svarṇapuṣpikā*;
all these, combined with *indragopaka* insects, should be placed into a vessel.
One should sweat it for seven days; therein, vaikrānta attains a state of liquefaction.
Likewise, among the eight metals, liquefaction occurs through the application of *vajra* and sweating.
There is no doubt that this occurs through the power of this yoga;
for this king of yogas performs the supreme liquefaction of gems.
Having placed the various liquefied substances separately in the midst of safflower oil, they will remain for a long time; when the occasion arises, one should employ them.

The wearing of gems is declared to always remove the afflictions caused by the sun and other planets, bestow long life, health, the rise of good fortune, luck, subjugation of others, wealth, and energy, grant fortitude, and take away the misfortune arising from contact with ill-omened shadows or moving dust; it destroys the influence of malevolent spirits and the like.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purification and Other Processes of Gems," in the *Rasaratnasamuccaya* composed by Ācārya Vāgbhaṭa, son of the venerable Vaidyapati Siṃhagupta.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
[Now, regarding metals:
Now, the qualities of gold—
Pure metal consists of gold, silver, copper, iron, and the essence of stone (steel); two types of base metal are mentioned, known as lead and tin.

Three types of mixed metal are mentioned: brass, bronze, and bell-metal. In the context of metals, *luha* is considered a synonym for *dhātu* (metal), and it also signifies the measure of one *karṣa*.

Gold is traditionally said to be of five kinds: that which is natural, that which is innate, that produced from fire, that produced from a mine, and that born from the alchemical transmutation of mercury.

Gold, born of the Ganges, bestows longevity, fortune, splendor, intelligence, and memory; it destroys all diseases, is meritorious, pacifies possession by spirits, grants the bliss of love's fullness, and illuminates happiness and nourishment. Silver likewise removes disease, prevents old age, cures urinary disorders, provides nourishment for the emaciated, clarifies the intellect, and increases virility. (VR 5.3)
That by which the universe is indeed enveloped, born from the quality of rajas,
is called the "Prakritic" (prākṛta), which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
That golden membrane with which Brahmā was born enveloped has become the form of Mount Meru;
for that gold is indeed innate to him.
The unbearable Śiva-like splendor emitted by Agni was swallowed;
all that was thus designated became gold born from fire.
This divine triad of colors, endowed with sixteen qualities,
shall by its mere wearing make the body free from old age and death.
Whatever is produced in the mines of various mountains,
enriched with the fourteen types of minerals, when consumed, removes all diseases.
That which is produced by the transmutation (vedha) of the lord of mercury is declared to be "born of transmutation" (vedhaja);
for that born of transmutation is indeed the most excellent elixir (rasāyana), supremely pure.
It is unctuous, pure, a destroyer of poisons and fevers, nourishing, and the foremost among aphrodisiacs;
it is supreme in pacifying insanity and possession, a crusher of bodily diseases, a producer of intellect,
understanding, memory, and happiness, and a destroyer of all humors and ailments.
Gold is palatable, digestive, pacifies disease, and has a sweet post-digestive effect.
Impure gold destroys happiness, vigor, and strength, and causes a multitude of diseases; therefore, one should employ gold that has been purified by smelting.

A gold leaf weighing one *karṣa*, enclosed within a crucible and combined with sharp metallic substances, remains for half a watch (*prahara*) in a bed of charcoal; by means of blowing [upon it], it will indeed become full of color.
The killing of all metals is best accomplished by means of mercury-ash;
they say it is middling when done with root-herbs, and inferior when done with sulfur and other such substances.
The killing of iron with copper imparts undesirable qualities.
Having made gold leaves that can be pierced by a thorn, one should coat them with mercury mixed with the ash of *luṅga* fruit; it is killed after ten *puṭa* applications.
One should cast the dead mercury, measured according to the weight of the gold, into the molten gold;
it should be powdered with citron juice and combined with cinnabar.
Gold acquires the luster of saffron after twelve cycles of heating and quenching.
Having smeared a quarter-part of mercury upon gold that has been ground with some acid, one should cook it in eight *puṭa* applications; thus it certainly becomes fixed (*mṛta*).
By means of a counter-addition (prativāpa) of frog-bone, fat, borax, *hayalālā*, and *indragopa* insects,
gold remains in a molten state for a very long time.
Powdered *surendragopa* insects, processed with the juices of *devadālī* fruits,
quickly turns base metal into gold resembling [pure] gold, like water [turning iron into steel].
This ash, produced from gold and combined with pungent ghee, when licked in a dose of two guñjās, destroys consumption, loss of digestive fire, emaciation, dyspnea, cough, and anorexia in men;
it increases the essence of the bodily constituents (*ojas*), bestows strength, and eradicates the disease of jaundice (*pāṇḍvāmaya*).
It is wholesome, removes all poisons, destroys the effects of poison, and cures malignant planetary influences, indigestion, and other ailments.
[Interpolation] It robs men of their strength and vigor, and as it were incites a multitude of diseases within the body;
always causing unhappiness, impure gold, being defective, brings about death.
Now, regarding silver:
it is considered to be of three kinds—naturally occurring, produced from mines, and artificial.
Indeed, each preceding type of silver possesses superior qualities compared to each subsequent one.
Silver produced from mountains such as Kailāsa is innate;
indeed, its mere touch once destroys the diseases of embodied beings.
Having examined all the treatises on alchemy in their proper order,
this [work] is now being revealed for the benefit of practitioners.
Without the ritual sequence there is no scripture, and without the scripture there is no sequence;
he who, having understood the scripture as endowed with the sequence, performs [the rite], is a possessor of accomplishment.
The preceptor was possessed of knowledge, skillful, and an expert in the science of alchemy;
he was perfected in mantra, a great hero, steadfast, and devoted to Śiva.
One who is devoted to the Goddess, ever steadfast, intent upon the sacrifice to the deity,
a knower of the distinctions of all the scriptures (āmnāyas), and skilled in the work of alchemy—
endowed with such characteristics, he shall be a teacher of the science of mercury (rasavidyā).
Devoted to their gurus, of virtuous conduct, truthful, firm in their vows, free from laziness, knowers of their own duty, and always observers of the commands [of their teachers].
Free from deceit and envy, initiated into the traditional practices of their lineage,
supremely accomplished, tranquil, and devoted to the propitiation of the mantra— disciples endowed with such characteristics shall be suitable for the attainment of the *sūta*.
In that work of alchemy, assistants who are diligent, superior to the disciples,
of noble birth, and devoted to their master should be employed.
Those who are nihilists, of wicked conduct, and kissers of their teacher's wife, who desire to acquire knowledge through theft, deceit, and the revelry of the base; VRs 6.8.
For them, nothing whatsoever—be it jewels, mantras, or medicinal herbs—is successful;
if they employ these out of delusion, they only destroy their own wealth.
There is no happiness for them in this world, nor likewise in the next.
Therefore, when the Guru is satisfied solely by the power of devotion,
then that [instruction] should be received by the disciple for the sake of attaining the realization of the science of rasa;
having obtained the boon through the joining of hands and heads, one should practice it well.
In a delightful region free from affliction, under the righteous rule of Dharma,
in a prosperous and auspicious city inhabited by Umā and Maheśvara.
In that place, a wise person should perform the practice of the king of essences (rasarāja) in an exceedingly beautiful grove adorned with four gates.
There, a hall should be constructed, very spacious and beautiful,
provided with well-placed windows and adorned with divine paintings.
Near that, on level and well-illuminated ground, a rasa-maṇḍapa should be constructed—
extremely well-concealed, very spacious, and adorned with doors and bolts.
It was enriched with banners, parasols, and canopies, hung with garlands of flowers,
and resounded with the sounds of kettledrums, cymbals, bells, and horns.
The ground there should be made level, very firm, and like a mirror;
in its center, a beautiful altar endowed with the proper characteristics should be constructed.
Three niṣkas of gold leaf and nine niṣkas of mercury should be rubbed with an acidic liquid for one watch (yāma); with that, one should fashion the linga.
One should cook [the substance] contained in a citron within a decoction of *sāra* resin using a swing-oven (*dolāyantra*) for one day;
there, one should worship that *liṅga* with most auspicious offerings.
Whatever fruit results from the perfect worship of a thousand million lingas,
that fruit shall be multiplied ten million times by the worship of a liṅga made of mercury.
Indeed, thousands of killings of Brahmins and tens of thousands of killings of cows perish at that very moment from the sight of the Rasaliṅga.
"It is true, as Śiva has declared, that liberation is attained through touch;
one should worship with the King of Mantras, the venerable Ghorarāja, in the southeast."

One should contemplate [the deity] as having eighteen arms, white in color, five faces, and three eyes; mounted upon a corpse, blue-throated, and possessing a linga of the nature of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Upon his lap, one should visualize the Great Goddess, who has one face and four arms;
she holds a rosary and a goad in her right hands, and a noose and the gesture of fearlessness in her left hands;
she has the luster of molten gold and wears yellow garments.
The syllable *Śrī* (Śrīm) consists of speech; the seed-syllable of the power of Kāmarāja is *Rasāṅkuśā*.
Those by whom these twelve are mastered together are to be known as Śaivas; this is the Vidyā known as Rasāṅkuśā.
With this [mantra], one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth;
and one should worship Nandin, Bhṛṅgin, Mahākāla, and Kulīra in the order of the directions starting from the east, using their name-mantras preceded by *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
In this manner, daily worship should be performed there for the sake of attaining mastery over the elixir.
The science of alchemy (rasavidyā), as taught by Śiva, should indeed be imparted to the practitioner by a teacher who is joyful in spirit, according to the prescribed injunctions.
At an auspicious moment, under a favorable constellation, and endowed with the strength of the moon and stars,
he [placed] a water-filled jar joined with gold, gems, and fruits.
One should place [the vessel] before a mercury-liṅga wrapped in a divine cloth,
and worship it well with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, and food offerings.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) in a well-characterized yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
using sesame seeds, clarified butter, milk-rice (pāyasa), and flowers such as the *śatapuṣpā*, each separately.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should summon the disciple with the Aghora mantra and the Rasāṅkuśī mudrā—
the disciple who is united with the power of Kālinī and is devoted to the attainment of the perfection of mercury.
She whose hair is curled, who is dark-complexioned and lotus-eyed,
well-formed, youthful, broad-hipped, and auspicious— she is distinguished.
Her heart was agitated; she was bent low by the weight of her full breasts;
she was tender in her kisses, embraces, and touch, and soft-spoken.
Adorned with a vulva resembling a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree,
that woman who bears flowers during the dark fortnight is known as Kālinī;
she is supreme for the binding of mercury, its application, and in the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
In the absence of that [elixir], any beautiful young woman should be given sulphur mixed with ghee,
one *karṣa* at a time, for three weeks starting from dawn; she will then become equal to Kālinī.
Thus, the best of gurus, endowed with power, should initiate him;
having bathed well, he should consecrate him with the mantra using the waters from the ritual jar.
The true guru should bestow the Aghorā-aṅkuśī-vidyā upon the disciple;

the fee for the guru (gurudakṣiṇā) should be given by the good disciple according to his capacity. Then, by the command of the guru, one should recite each mantra separately one hundred thousand times.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ, O Aghora, manifest, manifest, become clear, become clear, speak, speak, pacify, pacify, arise, arise, burn, burn, strike down, strike down! Oṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hrūṃ, to Aghora, phaṭ! By the command of Oṃ Kāmarāja-Śakti-Bīja-Rasāṅkuśā, [I invoke] this Aghora mantra, the Rasāṅkuśā Vidyā.
With this *aṅkuśavidyā*, one should worship the Goddess Śakti.
One should offer oblations ten times the [number of] recitations into a triangular fire-pit measuring one cubit;
using jasmine flowers smeared with the three sweets, and at the conclusion of the final oblation, there is the worship of a maiden.
Then, having prepared a clean hall smeared with plaster and provided with an altar,
one should draw there a two-cubit hexagonal mandala using vermilion.
One should correctly draw [the mandala] upon the altar, and outside of that, an eight-petaled lotus and a square adorned with four gates.
Upon the pericarp, one should place a crucible made of iron and inscribed with gold;
in its center, one should worship the king of essences (rasarāja) in a quantity of exactly one hundred palas,
or fifty, or twenty-five, as if it were a liṅga of mercury.
One should worship in sequence within the hexagon these six: diamond, vaikrānta, vajra, abhraka, antapāṣāṇa, and ṭaṅkaṇa; as well as bhūnāga and the śaktis.
Gandha, tālaka, kāsīsa, śilā, kaṅkuṣṭha, bhūṣaṇa,
rājāvarta, and gairika— these are known as the secondary minerals (uparasas).
These eight are to be worshipped in the petals, proceeding in order from the east to the northeast.
Rasaka, vimalā, tāpya, capalā, tuttha, añjana, hiṅgula, and sasyaka— these are known as the great minerals (mahārasas).
One should worship them on the tips of the petals, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
At the eastern gate are gold and silver; at the southern, copper and lead; at the western, tin and magnetite; and at the northern, muṇḍaloha and tīkṣṇaloha.
One should worship all of these, together with the goad, using the Aghora mantra.
Vitriol, vinegar-machines, alkalis, clay, and salts;
crucibles, retorts, blowpipes, chaff, charcoal, and sandstone.
A bellows, various staffs, a stone, a mortar, and a pestle;
the tools of a goldsmith, and all types of scales.
Various vessels made of clay, wood, copper, and iron,
as well as groups of divine medicinal herbs, dyes, and unguents—
these one should worship outside the door with the root mantra.
The five-syllable mantra is *vāṅmāyā* (vāṃ), *hrīṃ*, followed by *kṣeṃ* and *kṣma*.
With this mantra, one should worship Bhairava there;
at that time, one should proclaim the names of all those who have attained mastery over mercury (*rasasiddha*).
Vyālācārya, Candrasena, Subuddhi, Naravāhana, Nāgārjuna, Ratnaghoṣa, Surānanda, and Yaśodhana.
Indra, Māṇḍavya, Carpaṭī, Śūrasenaka, Āgama, Nāgabuddhi, Khaṇḍa, and Kāpālika are considered [the teachers].
Kāmāri, the Tantrika, Śambhu, Laṅkālampaṭa, Śārada, the Asura Bāṇa, the best of sages, Govinda, Kapila, and Bali.
All these lords of sūtas, accomplished in mercury and possessed of great strength,
wander through all the worlds, eternally devoted to worldly enjoyments.
The twenty-seven physicians who bestow the accomplishment of mercury (rasasiddhi) should be honored with diligence; thereafter, one should perform the worship of mercury.
Gladdening the twice-born and the gods, he should satisfy his chosen deities;
he should satisfy and worship with devotion, according to his capacity, the maidens, the yoginīs, the lords of yogins, and the practitioners of the melaka.
Thus, one should perform the festival of the elixir (rasotsava) endowed with all the necessary provisions;
this serves to pacify all obstacles and bestows the fruits of all that is desired.
Otherwise, that deluded soul who, devoid of a guru, desires to perform the practice of the elixir without the sequence of mantra-initiation, [will fail].
One does not attain success even through hundreds of millions of efforts;
therefore, with every exertion, one should perform the ritual actions prescribed in the scriptures.

Those who possess correct means of accomplishment, are diligent, associated with a guru, adorned by the king’s command, averse to various worldly activities, devoted to the mercury (*rasa*), wealthy, sought after by people, skilled in the work of measuring, apparatuses, and proper cooking, and expert in all medicinal herbs— for them alone, through the power of the prescribed ritual, does the glorious mercury (*pārada*) succeed, and not otherwise.
The science of alchemy (rasaśāstra) should be imparted to Brahmins for the sake of dharma;
to a king or a Vaiśya for the sake of prosperity; and to others for the sake of servitude.
When the Guru is pleased, Śiva is pleased; when Śiva is pleased, Rasa is likewise pleased.
When Rasa is pleased, all ritual actions (kriyās) are accomplished without a doubt.
The science of alchemy must be kept strictly secret, as surely as a mother’s private parts;
it remains potent when concealed, but becomes powerless through disclosure.
A task should not be undertaken merely because it is known by the patient, nor likewise because it is known by many; for medicine known by many patients becomes devoid of its potency.
One should construct a laboratory for alchemy (rasaśālā) in a delightful place free from all disturbances, abounding in all medicinal herbs, and provided with a well.
In the beautiful quarters of the Yakṣa, Tryakṣa, and Sahasrākṣa,
it was well-adorned with various implements and graced by a magnificent wall.
One should install Rasabhairava in the eastern part of the hall;
fire-related rites in the southeast, and stonework in the south.
One should perform surgical operations in the southwest, cleansing and so forth in the west,
drying in the northwest, and likewise the rite of piercing in the north;
one should perform the installation of accomplished objects in the northeast corner.
One should prepare a collection of substances for the purpose of accomplishing the *rasa*,
as well as a very beautiful *sattvapātana* crucible and a *jharat* crucible.
There were many earthen pits, moving baskets, and water-tubs;
likewise, there were pairs of bellows for both bamboo and iron at the furnace.
He should likewise collect various tools for goldsmiths, blacksmiths, brass-workers, copper-smiths, stonemasons, and leather-workers, as well as their raw materials.
There were small mortars and pestles, round wooden troughs,
iron pans heated for roasting, and likewise various kinds of grinding stones.
The *cālanī* (sieve), which is provided with thousands of fine holes for the purpose of straining substances,
as well as the *kaṭatrāṇi*, the *śalākā*, and the *kuṇḍalī*.
The winnowing fan is said to be of three kinds, and its nature is now described:
that which is constructed from bamboo strips and bound together with cords is always proclaimed to be beneficial for winnowing coarse substances.
And for the purpose of stirring the powder, there was another churning-stick made of bamboo.
It was fashioned from the heartwood of the *karṇikāra*, the *śālmali*, and the *harijāta* tree,
measuring four finger-breadths in width, and was auspicious.
A winnowing basket with a wide opening made of precious *kuṇḍalī* grass, wrapped in goat skin,
its base bound with horse-hair cloth—
by means of this one should perform the winnowing in order to remove even the subtlest dust.
Melted lead, clay, chaff, cotton, wood, stone, flour,
as well as medicinal substances consisting of minerals, living organisms,
and roots; likewise, fire, cow-dung, sugar, and white sugar.
The peacocks are considered to be the remnants of the fire, while the cuckoos are regarded as its embers.
The cuckoos were like extinguished coals, quenched without water.
Piṣṭaka, chagaṇa, chāṇa, upala, utpala, giriṇḍa,
upalasāṭhī, and saṃśuṣkacchagaṇa are synonyms for dried cow-dung fuel.
And small jars and drinking cups made of glass, iron, clay, and cowrie shells.
Kūpikā, kupikā, siddhā, golā, and giriṇḍikā.
Caṣaka, kaṭorī, vāṭikā, khārikā,
kañcolī, and grāhikā— these are indeed synonyms with a single meaning.
Winnowing baskets, bamboo vessels, small helmets, conch-shell trumpets, razor-edged arrows, as well as cooking pots, and whatever else is appropriate there;
small bowls, ear-rings, and knives for cutting vegetables.
Indeed, all work beginning with the sweeping of the halls and ending with the cooking of the broth,
as well as whatever else is useful therein— all that [is accomplished] by means of the supreme knowledge.
Having consulted with Śrīrasāṅkuśā regarding everything, one should perform the worship;
otherwise, the Bhairavas seize the splendor residing therein.
Physicians who contemplate the properties of tastes, those learned in the Nighaṇṭus, commentators,
and those who understand the languages of all countries— these too should be gathered by practitioners.
For one should always cause the recitation of the Aghora mantra until the completion of the digestion of the elixir.
The attendants were industrious, pure, brave, and very strong.
One who is most righteous, truthful in speech, learned, a worshiper of Śiva and Keśava,
compassionate, and lotus-handed should be employed in the science of alchemy (rasavaidyaka).
One who has on his hands the marks of a banner, a water-pot, a lotus, a fish, and a bow,
and whose ring finger is marked by a line below it, shall possess a hand that holds the nectar of immortality.
A physician who lacks instruction, is devoid of compassion, is greedy, has abandoned his teacher,
and draws black lines [on the patient's body] is said to have a "burnt hand."
Those who know the mantras for subjugation should be employed in the accomplishment of the treasure.
Those who are powerful, truthful, red-eyed, and dark-bodied,
and who possess the knowledge for terrifying spirits— these should be employed in the accomplishment of the *bali* offering.
Those who are free from greed, speakers of truth, worshippers of the gods and Brahmins,
self-controlled, and eaters of wholesome food, should be employed in the practice of alchemy (*rasāyana*).
They will be wealthy and generous, endowed with all necessary utensils;
always devoted to the words of their gurus, they will be auspicious in the practice of alchemy.
Those who know the names of various medicines, who are pure and free from deceit,
and who understand the languages of diverse regions, are considered fit for the procurement of medicinal herbs.
The essence [of the teaching] is always perfected for those who are pure, who speak truthful words, who are full of faith, who are high-minded,
and whose minds are free from doubt.
Having attained perfection through the tenfold eightfold practice, that supreme adept [should know]: "Alas! The mercury is lost! Having said this, he should consume that mercury elsewhere.
A mortal who has attained mastery over the elixir becomes a giver and an enjoyer, not a beggar;
freed from old age, honored by the world, possessing divine luster, he is forever happy.
Sōmadeva relates this technical terminology of mercury for the awakening of simple-minded physicians,
as it has been proclaimed by perfected scriptures.

Half [of the dose] is of the perfected elixir (*siddharasa*), one-eighth part is of the linctus (*leha*) made of oil and ghee, and likewise, one-seventh part is of all well-prepared iron powders, pills (*vaṭaka*), and so forth; that which is given by those afflicted with disease to the best of physicians after invoking Dhanvantari for the attainment of total health and happiness—that portion is declared to belong to Dhanvantari.
Even that eleventh portion of the goods purchased for medicine which is taken from the merchants by physicians is called the "share of Rudra."
That physician who, having greedily seized a portion of the patient's wealth, administers improper medicine with a covetous mind, shall be a betrayer of trust.
The mercury, when rubbed with non-fluid minerals such as sulphur and the like until it becomes very fine and resembles collyrium, is designated as *kajjalī*.
Those very same excellent substances, when ground together, are known as "mercury-paste" (rasapaṅka).

Then, from mercury equal to one-twelfth part of *arka*, and from sulphur equal to half a *niṣka*, one should grind them little by little in a mortar under intense sunlight; thus it becomes a paste with the appearance of butter.
Having ground mercury with fragrant substances and milk in a mortar, it reaches a state of being a paste through pounding; that is considered "piṣṭī" by others.
When sixty *ghṛṣṭis* are performed with mercury and a fourth part of gold, that becomes a *pātanapiṣṭī*; it bestows the supreme accomplishment upon the mercury.
Silver or gold, when afflicted by defects such as impurities in its taste or smell, undergoes many transformations; that process is known as *kṛṣṭī* for both gold and silver.
One should add a paste of gold; by that means, its color does not diminish.
The seed of mercury is prepared by means of gold extraction for the purpose of coloring it.
Copper, joined with iron, having been repeatedly melted and cast into the liquid extract of *gandha* and *lakucha*, emerges as excellent metal (*varalohaka*).
Gold colored by that [mineral] is called *hemarakti*.
Cast into molten gold, it imparts excellence of color;
it also serves to dye silver and produces the coloring of seeds.
In this very way, one should fashion a beautiful, red-colored *tāra* [bead],
which indeed dyes silver and even dyes seeds.
When another metal is processed with mercury— whether dead, bound, or otherwise— or with other metals,
such that it attains a white or yellow state, that indeed is known as the "petals" (dala) of the Moon and Fire.
Combined with mercury processed for a month and bound [into pills],
or prepared with another metal, it becomes white or yellow according to its portion.
Copper killed with honey and raised ten times, as well as purified lead—these two, each weighing four palas; VRs 8.19.
When blue collyrium has been applied to it seven times and it rises [to the surface] once more,
this is indeed called "perfectly accomplished" (saṃsiddha) lead-copper (śulvanāga).
The lord of elixirs (sūtendra), having been prepared by him, when held in the mouth of men,
specifically destroys the entire host of urinary disorders within a single month.
By eating wholesome food for a year, one becomes endowed with all health, possessing a vulture’s vision and radiant vigor, along with the fading of gray hair and wrinkles.
When iron is cast into another molten metal, heated, and then quenched,
it acquires a pale yellow luster and is called *piñjarī*.
The sixteen parts of the moon and the twelve parts of the sun,
when combined together, are therefore called "Moon-Sun" (Candrārka).
If another metal is cast into the metal being processed through the blowpipe,
that is indeed called *nirvāpaṇa* by physicians, or rather *nirvāhaṇa*.
One should cast the substance for extinguishing into that which is to be extinguished in equal proportions;
likewise, when the portion to be invoked and sown is observed, it is treated as previously described.
That which causes even a corpse to float upon the water is indeed iron that floats on water.
That which, when rubbed between the thumb and forefinger, enters the space between the lines,
is designated as "dead metal" (mṛtaloha) according to the terminology beginning with "lines" (rekhā).

When mixed with honey and clarified butter, it becomes as pleasant to the touch as jaggery and guñjā seeds; yet when smelted, it does not return to its original state—this is called "non-recurrence" (apunarbhava).
One should certainly place heavy objects and grain upon it;
it is proclaimed as the best method, for one crosses the water like a swan.
If that [iron], when heated together with silver,
should adhere to the silver, then that metal is said to be "irreversible" (niruttha), meaning it does not undergo rebirth.
When, through a specific process of quenching, it becomes that particular color, soft, and possesses variegated refinements, it is called a seed (*bīja*).
This indeed has been declared by physicians to be the cure:
the removal of one of two metals that have come into contact with each other. (VR 8.33)
When it is blown through a curved pipe, that is declared to be *tāḍana*.
Powdered mica combined with rice and bound in a cloth is placed in fermented rice-gruel (kāñjika);
when it has emerged from the cloth through rubbing, it is called dhānyābhra.
That essence which emerges from it after it has been heated in a furnace together with alkaline, acidic, and liquefying agents is called *sattva*.
A *kolīsaka* is considered to be one [unit] that reaches up to the neck when filled with fire-pits (*koṣṭhikā*) brimming with cuckoos (*kokila*) through the process of smelting.
For liquefaction and the falling of the essence, madhūka and khadira wood are auspicious;
for difficult liquefaction, bamboo is used, while for steaming, bādara wood is auspicious.
That mercury which is extracted from what resides within the machine known as the *vidyādhara*, having been rubbed with the juice of fresh ginger,
is indeed called "extracted by means of vermilion" (*hiṅgulākṛṣṭa*).
Bell-metal (kāṃsya) containing a small amount of tin, when struck with a blowpipe, releases its color;
that copper is indeed said to be "drawn by ghoṣa" (ghoṣākṛṣṭa).
That which is endowed with sharp black collyrium, when repeatedly and firmly smelted until it becomes black and flows like liquid, is called the "excellent nāga."
Furthermore, the re-emergence of one who has died is proclaimed by the name "raising up" (utthāpanā).
The pouring of a liquid into another liquid is considered *ḍhālana*.
Having ground thirty palas of nāga with the milk of a *bhānu* plant,
one should subject it to *puṭa* firing until only one *karṣa* remains.
Even with a thousand vessels of that [powder], this volatile substance produced from the naga would not be entirely exhausted; so it was declared by the commentators.
For in this way, even the Vaṅga [king] must undoubtedly be made fickle.
The *rasa* alone is bound when it is touched by the hand that has been touched by that [wind].
That mercury is praised in the alchemical treatises (*dhātuvāda*), not in the elixirs of longevity (*rasāyana*);
for this was proclaimed by the Lord of the World named Kharvaṇa.
When the dust is washed away with water mixed with the excrement of a cobra and the earth,
that which becomes black in color is called *dhauta* by the alchemists.
The union of two substances through rubbing and heating is proclaimed as *dvaṃdvāna*.
When there is an excess of the portion and so forth, the addition is made to the *anu* and *varṇa* syllables;
or else, the consumption by fire (*vahnikāgrāsa*) is considered by the masters to be the "breaking" (*bhañjanī*).
Goldness produced from the paste of *pataṅgī* in iron and silver persists for a few days and then vanishes; it is considered "transient" (*cullakā*).
For that which emerges from iron that has been heated for a long time, or from [other metals] after being smelted for a long duration,
is designated as *viniryāsa*, known by the name *pataṅgīrāga*.
Indeed, that which is the addition of another substance to iron and the like is called *āvāpa*; *pratīvāpa* is considered to be the very same thing, as is *ācchādana*.
When the iron is situated in the fire, one should pause for eight *nimeṣas* and then sprinkle water upon it; that is known as *abhiṣeka*.
The casting of the heated [metal] into water is called *nirvāpa* and *snapana*.
The addition of medicinal ingredients should be performed when the iron is molten and perfectly pure.
When the fire has blazing flames and is accompanied by the rising of smoke that is white, then it should be known as the *śuddhāvarta*; that is the time for the departure of the essence (*sattva*).
When a flame resembling molten metal is seen during smelting, this is the state of being ready for liquefaction;
it is called the "revolving of the seed" (bījāvarta).
That which is cool even while situated in fire is called "cool as one's own body."
That cold which is drawn out from fire is called external cold.
Indeed, the cooking of a substance placed in a *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus) with alkaline or acidic medicinal herbs is called *svedana* (sudation), which causes the loosening of impurities.
Grinding with rising medicinal herbs, along with all acidic substances and sour gruels (kāñjika), is called "rubbing" (mardana); it destroys external impurities.
That *mūrchana*, which causes the skin to become as fine as flour when treated with prescribed medicines such as *mardana* and others,
indeed destroys the scales of tin, lead, and snakes.

Indeed, that which brings about the restoration of one's natural state through the application of sweating, exposure to heat, and so forth, is called "reviving" (utthāpana); it destroys fainting and physical collapse.
For that indeed is bondage because the essential nature is crushed by its destruction;
when the elixir has been conquered by the wise, it is said to have its "crushing" destroyed.

The extraction of mercury—which has been rubbed with prescribed medicinal herbs and placed within a vessel—upward, downward, or sideways, is called *pātana*; it destroys the impurities (*kañcuka*) produced by contact with tin and lead.
The retention of the juice mixed with water and rock salt inside a jar for three days is called *rodhana* (sealing).
For mercury that has acquired potency through confinement, sweating is performed to eliminate its volatility; indeed, that is declared to be "restraint" (niyamana).
Combined with minerals, stones, roots, and so forth, and placed inside a jar for three days for the purpose of consumption, this is considered by the wise to be *sveda*, which is known as *dīpana*.
The measure of food consisting of edible substances for a horse of this size,
which is stated to be "this much," is what is proclaimed as the "measure of a mouthful" (grāsamāna).
The ingestion of the morsel, its melting within the womb, and likewise its digestion—thus has the threefold digestion been described by the excellent commentators. (VR 8.72)
The mouthful, the morsel, and the transformation—these are the three designations; furthermore, there is the supreme one.
Furthermore, digestion (jāraṇā) is of two kinds: with face-to-face contact (samukhā) and without face-to-face contact (nirmukhā).
The "faceless" digestion (nirmukhā-jāraṇā) is said to occur by means of taking a portion of the seed (bīja).
Pure gold and silver are designated as "seed."
The casting of seed by sixty-four parts is called the "mouth."
When this is done, the mercury becomes possessed of a mouth, greedy for morsels;
it becomes capable of consuming even hard metals.
This is indeed called "mukhā" (mouthed) digestion by Mṛgacārin.
Through the application of divine herbs, he remains within manifest crucibles;
he who possesses the mouth of a Rākṣasa may consume all metals and other substances.
The consumption of the essence within the stomach by means of swallowing is considered *cāraṇā*.
The liquefaction within the womb of that which has been swallowed is declared to be "womb-liquefaction" (garbhadruti).

Having thus performed liquefaction externally with substances such as *ghanasattva* and the like for the purpose of digesting (*jāraṇā*) the lord of mercury (*rasendra*), that is called external liquefaction (*bāhyadruti*).
Stainlessness, fluidity, luminosity, lightness,
and non-attachment to the mercury— these are the fivefold characteristics of liquefaction.
Likewise, through the application of medicinal substances and blowing, iron, base metals, and so forth, come to exist in a liquid form;
that is proclaimed as *druti* (liquefaction).
The digestion of the molten mass through the application of the "feces-machine" (viḍayantra) and other such means is called *jāraṇā*; its varieties are in the tens of millions.

It is proclaimed as *viḍa* because it is used for the digestion of the swallowed essence (*rasagrāsa*) by means of alkaline substances, acids, fragrant materials and the like, as well as potent urines.
Indeed, the production of colors such as yellow and others in mercury through the digestion (*jāraṇa*) of well-perfected seeds, minerals,
and so forth, is proclaimed as "coloring" (*rañjana*).
The process in which gold and other substances are cast into a crucible containing oil and heated,
thereby increasing the penetration [of the mercury] into the metal, is proclaimed as *sāraṇā*.
Indeed, when a liquid medicine possessing penetrating properties is infused into a substance, it is called *vedha* by those who know it; and that is said to be of many kinds.
The smearing, the hurling, the spear, the one called smoke, and the one known as sound.

When one performs a coating (*lepana*) so that iron becomes gold or silver, that is to be known as *lepavedha* (coating-penetration); and in this case, the *puṭa* (herbivorous vessel) used is the *sauraka*.
The casting [of mercury] into molten metal is known as *kṣepavedha*.
And that extraction of molten substances by means of a pair of tongs,
which effects their transformation into gold and so forth, is called *kuntavedha*.
When smoke arises within the fire from the fumes of the liquid cast inside,
the production of gold and other substances within the metal is called *vedha*.
Indeed, when a small amount of iron is blown with mercury held in the mouth,
the production of gold or silver is proclaimed as *śabdavedha* (piercing by sound).
The removal of impurities and the like from the perfected substance by means of mercury,
as well as the manifestation of its color, is declared to be its "unveiling" (udghāṭana).
Having sealed the vessel together with alkaline and acidic medicinal substances with great care, it is buried in the ground with effort; this is proclaimed as *svedana* (sudation).
The careful placement of mercury mixed with medicinal ingredients, contained within a vessel,
inside a hearth with a mild fire, is called *saṃnyāsa*.
These two methods of applying heat to the elixir-king are certain to produce its qualities and power, as well as to ensure its rapid pervasion [throughout the body].

Having gathered from all sides the jewels of the most lucid technical definitions from the great ocean of the *Rasāyanasaṃhitā*, Somadeva has with great effort fashioned this necklace for the throat; may the foremost of physicians wear it in the assembly for the sake of adornment.
This chapter shall be the recited authority for those who speak of alchemy;
one performing alchemical operations will not be deluded anywhere by it.
Now, having thoroughly examined them, Somadeva shall hereafter describe the alchemical apparatuses in their entirety and in brief.
Because mercury is diligently operated by masters of the *vārttika* to perform processes such as sweating (*sveda*),
it is known as a *yantra*.
Having filled a vessel halfway with a liquid substance and water,
one should carefully provide two openings on both sides of its mouth.
One should place a medicinal paste-pouch between those two rods, tie it fast, and subject it to steaming; this is known as the *dolāyantra* (swing apparatus).
One should place the substance to be cooked inside a cloth tied over the mouth of a water-filled vessel;
that apparatus by which it is cooked after being covered is called a *svedanīyantra* (steam-distillation apparatus).
Below the throat, there is a reservoir for water, eight fingers in circumference, ten fingers in width, and four fingers in height.
One should insert its mouth into the opening of another vessel placed above it,
which has a back surface sixteen finger-breadths wide.
Having smeared the two sides with buffalo milk, flour, *maṇḍūra*,
and treacle, one should dry the joint and pour water into the reservoir;
this should then be placed upon a hearth— this is called the *pātanāyantra*.
Then, the wise one should carefully cause a heated iron stone to fall downward into the water placed within the smeared upper vessel.

Having placed a wide-mouthed jar or a broken pot into the middle of a vessel filled with water, the mercury (sūta) should be prepared in a crucible and placed upon it, situated in the midst of cow-dung.
Having covered it with a small iron saucer whose six joints have been sealed with clay,
one should [place it] in the middle of the previously mentioned pot and lid using charcoal made from *khadira* and *kola* wood.
Through sweating and massaging, the mercury situated in the tortoise-press digests;
then, by the power of fire alone, all the essences within the womb melt.
That upon which the mercury falls— situated within a tortoise-shaped apparatus on an earthen pedestal containing a lamp— is called the *dīpikāyantra*.
One should insert a bamboo tube into a hole below the neck of the vessel;
having made two bronze bowls into a hollowed-out pair filled with water.
A firm tube should be joined there, and one should have it made so;
the mercury, previously placed therein with the appropriate substances, [is drawn up] into that jar.
Heated by fire, [the liquid] rises from the tube and falls downward into that water;
for as long as the entire vessel remains hot, the collection of the essence occurs. This is called the *ḍekīya* machine.
Having prepared two iron crucibles measuring twelve finger-breadths in size,
one should place the one provided with a slight opening there, together with sulfur.
One should place that [substance] into another crucible containing mercury;
there shall be water beneath the mercury, while fire is kindled above and below.
O blessed lady, one should carefully cause the juice of garlic, strained through a cloth with effort,
to be administered in abundance after having thoroughly saturated the mercury and sulphur.
Having covered the vessel with another firm vessel placed above it,
one should carefully seal the joint with clay and cloth.
One should always apply a *kapota*-type seal within another vessel using a fire of one *karṣa* weight;
beneath the apparatus, one should provide either a fire of dried cow-dung or a fierce fire.
One should perform this for three days, and thereafter release the machine;
one should not perform a cooling procedure in hot water or on a heated hearth.
Therein the mercury is not consumed, nor does it go anywhere;
and by this very sequence, one should perform the digestion (*jāraṇā*) of the sulphur-born [mercury].
The *yantra* should be known as the Vidyādhara, formed from the union of two vessels;
having made the hearth four-faced, one should place the vessel containing the *yantra* upon it.
Having cast medicinal herbs into it, one should seal the opening of the vessel;
this is proclaimed by those learned in the tantras as the machine known as the *vidyādhara*.
Fire is above and water is below, while the collection of essences is in the middle;
this is declared to be Somanala, which causes the sky and the other elements to digest.
I shall now describe the crucible (garbhayantra), which produces ash from fine powder;
it is four finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width.
One should have a very firm crucible made of clay with a circular opening;
twenty parts of salt and one part of guggulu [should be used].
Having ground it very finely, again and again, repeatedly,
one should apply a firm coating to the crucible with salt, half-clay, and water.

The knower of the proper measure should draw it out from the ground with a fire of husks and gently sweat it for one day and night or for three nights; thus the mercury (rasendra) shall attain the state of ash.
Having filled one shallow pan with sand,
one should place another shallow pan upon it and cook it there slowly over a mild fire.
Likewise, with the five alkalies, urines, salt, and viḍa salt—
that is known as the haṃsapāka apparatus by the best of alchemists.
One should fill with three parts [of liquid] a glass jar that has a narrow mouth, is wrapped in soft cloth and fingers, and has been dried out.
In a vessel one span deep, well-supported with sand,
one should fill that vessel with three [parts] and cover it with others.
One should coat the mouth of the vessel with clay, join it to the *maṇikā* (the outer jar),
and bake it on a stove until the back of the *maṇikā* is heated but not scorched;
this indeed is the *vālukāyantra*, and that same apparatus may also be based upon salt.
Having carefully placed the mercury-globule and other substances into a vessel filled with five *āḍhaka* measures of sand, it is heated; this is described as the *vālukāyantra*.
Thus, by means of the casting of salt, the salt-mechanism (lavaṇayantraka) has been explained.
And having smeared the mouth of the copper vessel— which has been coated internally with *rasāla*—
and the joint of the base of the jar with earth and salt;
Having filled that vessel with alkaline substances, one should cook it as before;
thus it becomes a salt-yantra, which is highly recommended for the work of processing mercury (rasa).
Mercury placed within a metal tube, sealed inside a vessel filled with salt, should be cooked as before; this is described as the *nālikāyantra*.
One should fill a crucible containing mercury with sand covering all its parts, place it in a pit, and cover it with glowing stones; that apparatus is called the *bhūdhara* (earth-bearer).

One who knows the proper measure of fire should place the mercury inside a pair of earthen saucers and cook it on a brazier for two watches (six hours) over cow-dung fuel; this is the *puṭayantra* method.
Sixteen finger-breadths in width and one cubit in length, even and uniform,
it is known as the *koṣṭhīyantra* for the purpose of casting metallic elements and living beings.
In that [place], there was a very small iron vessel with two rings on its sides;
such a vessel had a compartment threaded through those rings.
Having placed it upon the previous vessel, one should pour it into a small vessel;
then, having filled the large vessel with *kāñjika* sour gruel, the essence becomes thoroughly blended.
One should indeed heat it for two watches (six hours) for the purpose of raising the mercury;
this is the *valabhīyantra*, which bestows sixfold qualities upon the mercury.
In a vessel made of fine *kāntaloha* iron, the mercury becomes even more excellent in its qualities.
One should pour the liquid into a jar provided with a long, downward-pointing tube;
that tube should indeed be inserted into the interior of the belly of another jar.
Then, having properly sealed the openings of the two jars with clay,
one should ignite a fierce fire beneath the mercury-pot.
One should pour sweet, cool water into the other jar;
this is indeed called "horizontal pouring" (tiryakpātana) by the commentators.
A circular iron vessel with a curved top and an upright handle—
this is indeed the *pālikā* apparatus for the purpose of digesting mercury.
This water-wheel (ghaṭayantra) is said to have a reservoir for four prasthas of water and a circumference of four aṅgulas; it is known as that which provides irrigation.
Having fashioned a circular pit and placed a wrestler therein,
he set upon it an auspicious brick that had a hollow in its center, like the middle of the pit.
One should construct a rim one finger-breadth high all around the pit;
having cast the fetus into the pit, one should place a cloth over the mouth of the pit.
One should place sulfur there, seal the opening with a crucible-lid,
and properly seal the space between the crucible and the lid with clay.
A crucible made from forest stones should be provided, known as the "pigeon" (kapota) type, and not larger than that;
this is the brick-press (iṣṭikāyantra), and by means of it one should digest the sulphur.
Having placed one vessel upon another and properly sealed them together,
and having poured water into the upper vessel, one should ignite the fire below;
this is the Vidyādhara yantra for the purpose of extracting mercury from cinnabar.
Having placed an inverted vessel upon the vessel situated on the apparatus, one should seal it;
that apparatus is called the *ḍamaruka*, and it is beneficial for producing the ash of mercury.
One should make a pit in the middle of the wrestling arena; there, one should place mercury together with sulphur. Around the pit, one should construct a wall one finger-breadth high.
Then, one should properly cover it with a crucible shaped like a cow’s teat,
having sealed it thoroughly with clay mixed with water, according to the method now being described.

Iron filings that have been thoroughly rubbed with a decoction of *babbūlaka* and mixed with fine molasses powder are called "water-killed" (*jalamṛt*); indeed, they are truly difficult to penetrate with water.
Indeed, when lime, cloth, and brick-dust are mixed with the milk of a buffalo,
it becomes "fire-clay," which is truly capable of enduring the intense heat of fire.
Obstructed by this clay, the mercury is unable to move,
just as a man is held back by the mature love of a clever woman.
Nandī, Nāgārjuna, Brahmajyotis, and the lord of sages Śrī Somadeva alone know this on the surface of the earth; no one else does.
Then, having poured water [into the vessel], one should ignite a fire beneath it;
this is called the *nābhiyantra* by Nandin, the all-knowing.
By means of this, mercury is digested, as well as smokeless, pure sulphur.
The wise have described the *grastayantra* as a crucible that is filled with its own belly, perfectly round inside from beginning to end, and flattened at the base;
it has indeed been proclaimed by those who know mercury for the purpose of cooking the lord of elixirs (*sūtendra*). (VR 9.65)
Having placed copper or other metals into a vessel and sealed its opening with a lid, it is heated from beneath the vessel; this is known as the *sthālīyantra*.

Having fashioned an iron vessel eight finger-breadths wide and eight finger-breadths in height, one should place it there at the base of the neck, in the region of the throat-support, at a distance of one finger-breadth below the neck.
One should insert thin iron needles horizontally,
and upon them, one should place thin gold leaves.
One should place the vessel to be described right here beneath the leaf;
indeed, one should cover that vessel with another vessel turned upside down.
Having smeared the joints with clay, one should ignite the fire below;
by that, all the leaves are struck [into a mass] according to the prescribed method.
The mercury moves with speed and flows rapidly within the crucible;
indeed, it may be processed with sulphur, realgar, or mica, or with collyrium, or with dead snake.
The incense of gold leaves is proclaimed as the first;
for the sake of silver, one should fumigate silver leaves with dead mercury (mṛtavaṅga).
And one should fumigate with other appropriate secondary minerals as well;
this is called the fumigation apparatus for the preparation of substances used in the process of *jāraṇā*.
Having poured water into a large pot and tied a cloth tightly over its mouth,
one should place the substance to be steamed therein and seal its opening.
One should ignite a fire beneath the apparatus known as the *kanduka*;
wise men call this the *svedanīyantra*.
Alternatively, having poured water into a vessel and placed grass on top of it,
having cast the substance to be steamed inside and having fitted a lid upon it,
one should kindle a fire beneath; that apparatus is known as the *kanduka* (ball) machine.
The stone suitable for a mortar is blue, dark, glossy, firm, and heavy;
it should be sixteen finger-breadths in height and nine finger-breadths in width.
The rubbing stone (gharṣaṇī) should be twenty-four fingers long and twelve fingers wide;
or it may be twenty fingers long and ten fingers in height.
Its measurement should be known as that of a mortar (khalva), and it is excellent for the work of processing mercury.
The mortar-machine is said to be of three kinds for the easy grinding of mercury and other substances.
They should be made smooth and without protruding nipples, joined with a small figurine.

In height, it is indeed ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and equal in length to one-sixteenth of a finger (kalā); in width, it is ten finger-breadths and depressed by twelve of those same finger-breadths.

At the rim, it is two finger-breadths wide, exceedingly smooth, and shaped like a half-moon; the grinding surface is twelve finger-breadths long. This is considered the *khalva* for the sake of success.
In this [preparation], five palas of mercury (sūta) are to be rubbed for purification;
one should employ it in various other mortars according to the requirements of each specific case.
The *khalva* is twelve finger-breadths in width, made of an extremely smooth stone,
four finger-breadths deep, and polished smooth in the middle.
The *mardaka* is flat at the bottom and has a well-gripping tip at the top;
this *khallo*, however, is round and provides great comfort during massage.
The iron mortar (khalla) is nine finger-breadths in length and six finger-breadths in depth;
the pestle (mardaka) is eight finger-breadths long, and this is also known as the heated mortar (taptakhalla).
Having fashioned a furnace in the shape of a leather bag and filled it with charcoal,
one should place that bag upon it and blow at its side with a bellows.
When that paste is rubbed inside it and combined with alkaline and acidic substances, and then heated by fuming, it melts away with extreme velocity; of this there is no doubt.
When processed with *kāntaloha* iron, this mercury becomes ten million times more potent.
Indeed, the crucible is called *krauñcikā*, *kumudī*, *karahāṭikā*,
*pācanī*, and *vahnimitrā* by the alchemists (*rasavādibhiḥ*).
That which steals away the defects (doṣas) is called a crucible (mūṣā).
Its material cause would be either clay or iron.

A single *kākiṇī* coin that has escaped from the mouth of a crucible is better than even a hundred thousand [coins] for the proud, when obtained by bowing down before a wicked person. *dhik*! (Fie upon it! 10.4.
The binding of the crucible and its lid is called *bandhana* or *saṃdhilepana*;
it is also termed *andhraṇa*, *randhraṇa*, *saṃśliṣṭa*, and *saṃdhibandhana*.
Clay that is pale and coarse, or reddish-pale like sugar,
which can withstand prolonged heating, is highly recommended for the purpose of making crucibles;
in its absence, clay from an anthill or a potter's workshop is prescribed.
The clay that has been pounded with milk-husk, hemp, lime, horse-dung, iron,
and a rod shall indeed be suitable for the purpose of crucibles.
White stones, husks, burnt [substances], firebrands, hemp,
and earthen shards, along with slag, black clay, and the earth from a rat's burrow, should be mixed together.
Three parts of clay, two parts of hemp and lac, one part of burnt husks and stones,
and half a part of dross— having broken these into pieces, one should indeed fashion a vajra-mūṣā crucible for the extraction of the essence (sattvapāta).
Clay from an anthill, mixed with burnt charcoal and husks,
combined with the respective excrement and smeared with that same excrement.
The crucible prepared by her is called the *yogamūṣā*;
mercury processed in this [crucible] becomes superior in its qualities.
A crucible made of equal parts of *gārā*, *bhūnāga*, *dhauta*, hemp, and burnt husks,
kneaded with the milk of a female buffalo, is likewise [recommended].
The *krauñcikā* is indeed proclaimed to be merely a type of apparatus in its many forms;
a crucible fashioned from it is suitable for the liquefaction of diamonds.

A crucible made from black earth mixed with milk, six times its weight of cow dung, eight parts of ash, charcoal, and hemp, is called a *gāramūṣā*; by heating it for two watches (*yāma*), it does not melt even by fire.
Charcoal and husks equal in measure to [the metal], with four times that amount of clay,
and charcoal equal to the clay— all these combined constitute what is designated as the "excellent crucible" (varamūṣā), which can withstand a watch (yāma) of fire.
A crucible made from red clay free of stones,
prepared with the red group of substances and smeared with *kṣiti-khecarī*,
is called a *varṇa-mūṣā*; it is employed for the enhancement of color.
A crucible made from white clay free of stones, prepared with white-colored earth and smeared with *kṣiti-khecara*,
is called a silver crucible; it is employed for the enhancement of color.
Produced from various types of clay and smeared with various kinds of *viḍa*,
it is called a *viḍamūṣā* for the purpose of alchemical processes involving the body or metals.
A crucible made from equal parts of *gārā*, *bhūnāga*, and *dhauta*, along with husked hemp,
should be rubbed with buffalo milk.
For the *krauñcikā* is proclaimed in many ways as merely a type of crucible;
a crucible fashioned from it should be smeared with the blood of bedbugs.
And with the roots of *bālābdadhvani* and *vajradrāvaṇakrauñcikā*,
she, being afflicted by disease, endures fire for four watches through the application of a liquid extract.
When the crucible has become liquid at its opening due to the application of heating,
the brief removal [of the contents] that occurs is called the replenishing of the crucible (*mūṣāpyāyana*).
In a crucible shaped like an eggplant, there is a tube twelve finger-breadths long;
at the top, it is as firm as a dhatura flower, with its petals firmly closed together.
Eight finger-breadths long and provided with a hole, that is the "bottle-gourd crucible" (vṛntākamūṣikā);
by means of this, one should extract the essence from soft substances such as earthen shards.
The crucible that is shaped like a cow’s udder and has a lid provided with a spout is the "cow-udder" crucible;
it is used for the liquefaction and purification of substances.
The "malla-mūṣā" (crucible of wrestlers) has been described as that which is formed from the union of two malla vessels;
it is proclaimed for the purpose of steaming the juices and other substances of parpaṭī and similar herbs.
That which has the form of a potter's vessel, being both firm and thoroughly baked,
is called a "mature crucible" (pakvamūṣā) for the purpose of baking medicinal powders and the like.
Having the shape of a smooth sphere and containing the substances for sealing, it is called a *golamūṣā*; it quickly obstructs the flow of liquids.
That which is shaped like an elbow, gradually widening towards the top,
and thick like a large eggplant (sthūlavṛntāka), is known as the *mahāmūṣā* (great crucible).
It is used for the *puṭa* (roasting) and the melting of iron, *abhraka*, *sattva*, and other such substances.
A crucible shaped like a frog,
which is six finger-breadths in length and width, is known as a "frog-crucible" (maṇḍūkī-mūṣā).
Having buried this crucible in the ground, one should then apply the *puṭa* (heat) on top of it.
A crucible that is flattened at the base and circular, with a height of eight finger-breadths, is called a *mūṣalī* crucible;
it is beneficial for mercury bound to mica.
For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity and for the purification of those already matured, there are various types of furnaces;
their characteristics are now described.
It was one *hasta* in height, half that in length and breadth,
square in shape, and enclosed by walls made of clay.
On a single wall, one should make a door provided with a width of one span;
the door should be well-constructed, auspicious, and measured at one and a half spans.
A wall measuring one span (prādeśa) should be constructed beneath the threshold for the purpose of blowing [the fire], and likewise above the lintel (uttaraṅga) as is appropriate.
A door should indeed be made at the top, measuring one span;
then, having blocked the joint of the door with bricks and smeared it [with mortar].
Having filled it with firebrands, one should blow upon it with two bellows;
one should cast the firebrands and the blowing materials through the upper opening.
Furthermore, by repeatedly adding five *golās* of mineral essence (*sattva*) at a time,
this becomes a charcoal furnace for the extraction of the essence from ores.
On firm ground, one should dig an auspicious circular pit measuring one span;
then, in the middle of that, one should fashion another pit.
It should be provided with a depth and width of four finger-breadths,
extending from the pit to the edge of the ground, and equipped with a horizontal tube.
One should place a clay wheel-pan, slightly raised at the rim and sloping downward toward the outer trench,
provided with five holes, into the interior of the central pit.
Having filled the crucible with cuckoos [of mercury], one should blow it with a single bellows;
for this is the "Pātālakoṣṭhikā" (Subterranean Crucible), which precipitates the essence of soft substances,
as proclaimed by Nandin for those materials that cannot be accomplished by mere blowing.
It should be twelve finger-breadths deep and likewise one span (prādeśa) in width;
it should rise four finger-breadths above [the rim] and be provided with a ring.
One should place a crucible containing many holes upon a ring;
having placed fire-tongs there, one should heat it with a blowpipe. This is called the "Gārakoṣṭhī" furnace, which destroys refined metals.
A firm crucible made of clay from a rat's burrow, measuring one *aratni* in size, should be prepared;
its mouth facing downwards, with a tube of five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) inserted into that opening. This is called the "bent tube" (*vaṅkanāla*), which is prescribed for providing a firm blow.
A crucible is prescribed for the preparation of perfected elixirs and the like;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths at its base.
Equipped with a lateral blowing-nozzle, it serves to purify soft substances.
A *puṭa* (a sealed vessel for heating) is that which makes known the correct measure for the cooking of substances such as juices;
a cooking process that is either deficient or excessive is not desired, for medicine is beneficial only when well-cooked.
The non-recurrence of defects such as impurities in iron, the increase of its qualities, and its superiority therefrom;
its not sinking in water, and its fullness of lines arising from smelting—these result from the crucible.
From the crucible and the stone, there arises lightness, rapid pervasion, and digestive stimulation;
moreover, the quality of the metals is superior even to that of the processed mercury (sūtendra).
Just as fire may enter into stone through the application of external crucibles,
so too is the attainment of qualities in metals certain, by virtue of their being reduced to powder.
In a square pit two cubits deep and wide,
filled with a thousand wild blue lotuses, one should place the medicinal herbs for the process of sublimation (*puṭana*).
One should carefully place the obstructed [substance] upon the *piṣṭikā* in a *krauñcī* crucible;
one should then set half a thousand *vanotpala* flowers upon the *krauñcī*.
One should ignite the fire therein; this is known as the *mahāpuṭa*. VRrs_10.52 //
Square and hollowed out to the measure of a king’s cubit,
it should be filled with pebbles and gravel and placed up to its neck.
One should place a *kumudī* vessel filled with the substances for the *puṭa* there;
one should then insert mountain-clay (*giriṇḍa*) pieces equal to half a full *chagaṇa*.
This is called the "elephant-seal" (*gajapuṭa*), which bestows great medicinal qualities.
In this manner, when the vessel is filled with cow dung, it is called the Vārāha-puṭa.
A *puṭa* on the surface of the earth, measuring two spans in height and as wide at its base,
is known as a *kukkuṭaka-puṭa*.
When a vessel is placed on the ground and covered with eight pieces of dry cow-dung cake for the purpose of calcining mercury or metallic ash, it is called a *kapotapuṭa*.
Cow’s urine collected from within a cow-pen, dried and powdered cow dung, and cow’s droppings—
these are prescribed as the most excellent substances for the preparation of mercury.
Where a packet is offered either with cow-dung or with husks,
that is called a *govara-puṭa*, for the purpose of successfully preparing the ash of mercury (*rasabhasma*).
When a thick-walled vessel filled with husks and fitted with a crucible in its center is subjected to heating by fire, that is called a *bhāṇḍapuṭa*.
Indeed, it is covered above and below by *krauñcikā* plants,
and where there are heated sands, that is the *vālukāpuṭa* hell.
One should properly bury [the crucible] two finger-breadths deep in the earth;
where there is a lid on top, that is the crucible called *bhūdhara*.

Above [the fire], a sealed vessel (puṭa) should be made using sixteen-fold urine, husks, or cow-dung; that which is so prepared is called the *lāvaka* method, used for processing very soft substances.

When the number of *puṭas* has not been explicitly stated, those skilled in reasoning and discernment should determine the appropriate number of *puṭas* by considering the relative strength and weakness of the substance to be processed (*sādhya-dravya*) and then administer them.
Piṣṭaka, chagaṇa, chāṇa, utpala,
upala, giriṇḍa, upalasāṭhī, and varāṭī are synonyms for dried cow dung (chagaṇa).
Gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and iron—these six are natural metals; bell-metal and brass are artificial alloys.
Six types of salts are mentioned: sea salt, rock salt, biḍa salt, sauvarcala salt, romaka salt, and likewise cūllikā salt.
The three alkalis are declared to be barley-ash, sarjikā, and ṭaṅkaṇa.
The alkali of *palāśa* and *muṣkaka*, barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), *suvarcikā*,
and the alkali derived from sesame stalks— these combined constitute the "fivefold alkali" (*kṣārapañcaka*).
Clarified butter, jaggery, and honey are to be known as the "triple sweet" (madhuratrika).
[One should avoid] *kaṅguṇī*, *tumbinī*, *ghoṣā*, and that which arises from *karīra* and *śrīphala*; likewise, [that which arises from] *kaṭuvārttāka*, *siddhārtha*, *somarājī*, and *vibhītaka*.
Likewise, [one should take] seeds of *atasī*, *mahākālī*, and *nimba*, as well as those from *tila*,
*apāmārga*, *devadālī*, *dantī*, and the body of *tumburu*.
Likewise, having taken oil from aṅkola, unmatta, bhallātaka, and palāśa, one should employ it in the process of alchemical extraction (rasakarma).
The fat of the jackal and the frog, the fat produced from the tortoise,
that of the crab and the porpoise, and that derived from the cow, the pig, and man; likewise, the fat of the goat, the camel, the donkey, the ram, and the buffalo.
One should employ the urine of elephants, young camels, female buffaloes, donkeys, and horses;
and the menstrual flow of cows, goats, and ewes, as well as the seed of males.
Buffalo meat, water, curd, milk, and clarified butter with ghee—this is known as the "five buffalo" (māhiṣapañcaka). Likewise, there is the "five goat" (śāgalapañcaka).
Amlavetasa, jambīra, nimbuka, bījapūraka, cāṅgerī, sour chickpeas (caṇakāmla), amlīkā, kola, and pomegranate (dāḍima).
Ambaṣṭhā, tintiḍīka, nāgara, rasapattrikā,
and likewise karavanda— these others are proclaimed as the group of sour substances (amlavarga).
Among all [acids], sour chickpea (caṇakāmla) alone is praised; or sour cane-leaf (amlavetasa) alone is the best of the best for all [metals].
It is beneficial for the purification of mercury and the like, and for the processes of liquefaction and digestion. (VR 10.79)
The juice of jujube, pomegranate, wood-apple, *cullikā*, and *cukrikā* is designated as the "five sours" (*pañcāmlaka*); it is also called the "fivefold sour" (*amlapañcaka*).
Brick, red ochre, salt, ashes, and anthill earth—
these are proclaimed as the five types of earth by those skilled in the application of mercury (*rasa*).
Śṛṅgīka, kālakūṭa, vatsanābha, along with artificial poison and bile— this is proclaimed as the excellent group of poisons.
This is praised for the preparation of mercurial elixirs (*rasakarma*) as well as for the process of purifying its impurities;
however, if consumed improperly, it certainly kills.
Lāṅgalī, viṣamuṣṭi, karavīra, jayā, nīlaka, kanaka, and arka constitute the group consisting of secondary poisons (upaviṣa).
An elephant, a horse, a woman, a cow, a she-ass, a she-goat, a ewe, a female camel, an udumbara tree, an aśvattha tree, a bhānu tree, a nyagrodha tree, and a tilvaka tree. (VRs 10.85)
Dugdhikā, snugguṇa, and likewise uttamakaṇṭikā—
the milks of these are prescribed as the "milk group" among the [categories] beginning with taste.

Indeed, the purification of all metals is prescribed by means of smelting (*puṭana*) and smearing (*lepana*), using the excrement (*viṅgaṇa*) of a pigeon, a blue jay, a dove, a peacock, a vulture, or even a cock. (VRs 10.87)
Safflower, khadira, lac, mañjiṣṭhā, red sandalwood,
akṣī, bandhujīva, as well as karpūragandhinī and honey—
these are to be known as the "red group," which is highly coloring.
The *kiṃśuka*, the *karṇikāra*, and the two types of *haridrā*—
this is declared to be the yellow group for the ritual of the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*).
Tagara, kuṭaja, kunda, guñjā, jīvantikā,
and the bulb of the white lotus are declared to be the white group (śvetavarga).
Plantain, bitter gourd, the three myrobalans, blue water-lily,
reed, mud, green vitriol, and young mango— this is declared to be the black group (kṛṣṇavarga).

Furthermore, whatever substance has the nature of being capable of digestion (*jāraṇa*) should be diligently infused with groups of red substances and so forth, in order to indeed attain such a coloration. (VR 10.92)
This group is considered to be purified by means of glass, borax, and kṣipra.
It is called by the alchemists the destroyer of the impurities of bound mercury and of metals, and the eradicator of the defects of the *kāpālī* and *kaṅguṇa* [preparations].
Buffalo horn, ram's horn, *kaliṅga*, and seeds of *dhava* tree,
along with the bones of a hare— this formulation destroys the hardness of iron.
This group, consisting of jaggery, guggulu, guñjā, clarified butter, sāragha honey, and ṭaṅkaṇa,
is considered suitable for liquefying all metals and other substances that are difficult to melt.
All alkaline substances destroy impurities; acidic substances cleanse and digest; they counteract dullness and poisons; and unctuous substances produce lubrication.
Six *truṭis* make one *likṣā*, and six *likṣās* are said to be a *yūka*;
six *yūkas*, O lady of noble vows, are declared by you to be what is known as a *rajas*.
Six *rajas* are directly a mustard seed (*sarṣapa*), and that is proclaimed as a *siddhārtha*;
O Goddess of Gods, six *siddhārthas* are proclaimed to be one barley grain (*yava*).
Six barley grains make one *guñjā*; three *guñjās* are called a *valla*.
