Six *guñjās* are proclaimed to be one *māṣa*.
Twelve *māṣas* make a *tola*, and eight *tolas* constitute a *pala*.
Six atoms (aṇu) constitute a truṭi; six of those are said to be a likṣā;
six of those make a yūkā, and six yūkās are known as a particle of dust (rajas).
Six *rajas* are said to be one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*); six of those are declared to be one barley grain (*yava*).
One *guñjā* consists of six barley grains, while a *niṣpāva* consists of two *guñjās*.
Three guñjās make one *valla*; two *vallas* are said to be one *māṣa*.
Two *māṣas* make one *dharaṇa*, and two of those are known as a *śāṇa*, a *niṣka*, and a *kalā*.
Two *niṣkas* constitute a *vaṭaka*, and that is called a *kola*;
three *kolas* make a *tola*, and four *niṣkas* make a *karṣa*.
The *udumbara* is the size of a palm; the *suvarṇa* is a mouthful;
the *akṣa* is the size of a cat's paw; and the *śukti* is two palms.
Some know two *śukti*s to be one *pala*, while others know three *śukti*s to be so; that same measure is also called a *muṣṭi*, a *prakuñca*, and a *bilva*.
Two *pala*s make a *prasṛta*; two of those make a *kuḍava*, which is also called an *añjali*.
Two *kuḍava*s make a *mānikā*, and two *mānikā*s are known as a *prastha*.
Two *prasthas* make one *śubha*; those two make one *pātraka*; two *pātrakas* make one *āḍhaka*.
With four of those, there are the measures known as *ghaṭa*, *unmāna*, *nalva*, *nārmaṇa*, and *śūrpa*.
One hundred *palas* of fleeing [birds] is a *droṇa*;
four hundred *palas* is proclaimed as a *bhāra*.
Having examined the treatises such as the Rasārṇava, I have set forth here whatever is useful for alchemy; only a mere indication of the direction has been shown.
Now we shall fully describe the purificatory processes of the king of essences (rasarāja).
There may be sweating, followed by rubbing, fainting, reviving, preventing the falling [of the mercury], and fixing;
then there is inflaming, devouring the sky, measuring, transmutation, and thereafter liquefaction within the womb.

External liquefaction consists of the digestion of mercury (sūtaka) and the process of swallowing; thereafter come the work of *sāraṇā*, transference (*saṃkrāmaṇa*), and the method of piercing (*vedha*) into the body. Thus, the practice here is eighteenfold.
It should not be applied when a vital point has been severed, nor when [the area] has been cauterized with alkali or fire.
When purified, it endures mild fire, becomes malleable, and destroys diseases.
With steady force, it is beneficial for longevity and health when consumed by a strong digestive fire;
yet poison, fire, and impurity are the three innate defects.
In the [taste] rasa, they are respectively the causes of death, agony, and fainting.
The two metallic substances, lead and tin, cause dullness, flatulence, and leprosy.
Furthermore, other seven types of artificial (aupādhika) gems are proclaimed:
those born of the earth, those born of mountains, those born of water, and two kinds born of lead and tin.
These twelve defects in flavor have been declared by those expert in flavors.
Those born from the earth cause leprosy; those born from mountains cause indeed dullness;
and those born from water cause a mass of wind-disorders in lead and tin when they are rich in defects.
Parpaṭī, Pāṭinī, Bhedī, Drāvī, Malakarī,
Andhakārī, and Dhvāṅkṣī are to be known as the seven coverings (kañcukas).
Therefore, for the purpose of preparing the elixir, one should begin the work of alchemy, taking all necessary equipment and accompanied by skillful assistants.
Two thousand palas, or a thousand, or even a hundred;
or twenty-eight palas, or ten, five, or even one.

The purification of the *sūtaka* (mercury) should be performed with only half a *palā* [of mercury] on an auspicious day and under a favorable lunar mansion; then one should begin the process of refining the essence.
Having added the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the salts, the two types of sun-plant (sūrya), citraka, fresh ginger, and radish,
the mercury should be repeatedly steamed with sour gruel (kāñjika) for three days.
Having added the powder of house-soot and brick, as well as curd mixed with jaggery,
and combined with salt and *asurī*, one should throw it [into the crucible] and grind the mercury.
One should employ that substance as a sixteenth part of the quantity of mercury;
having added the mercury equal to that [substance], one should grind it for three days.
Likewise, one should take digested abhraka and similarly digested mercury;
for the sake of purifying the mercury, one should place them in a mortar and grind them together.
The pure [mercury] takes up the impurities, being rubbed at every morsel;
for that process known as "rubbing" (mardana) produces the qualities of mercury.
Gṛhakanyā destroys impurity, and triphalā destroys digestive fire;
citramūla destroys poison; therefore, one should diligently [use] these.
One should cause the mercury (sūtaka), mixed with the [specified] substances, to coagulate seven times;
thus coagulated, the mercury becomes free from defects.
After this purgation, the mercury, once thoroughly cleansed,
should thereafter be precipitated from the acidic decoction (kāñjika) in order to eliminate the defect of putrefaction.
Having made a paste with copper, one should cause it to fall into an upper vessel;
having abandoned tin and lead, the mercury becomes pure.
One should cause the paste to fall through the filter three times above and seven times below.
Having prepared a liquid extract (rasa) from triphalā, śigru, and śikhin, combined with salt and āsurī, one should make it into a paste and smear it onto the upper vessel;
then, one should cause the [substance] to fall downward by means of glowing blue lotuses.
With turmeric, *aṅkola*, *śampāka*, *kumārī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *agni*;
with *taṇḍulīyaka*, *varṣābhū*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), rock salt (*saindhava*), and honey; [these are used for the treatment].
O Goddess, one may cause [the discharge] to fall by using ground juice with salt and *sarpākṣī* and other such herbs,
or else with *yakṣalocana* which destroys wounds.
For when he has thus been cast down by falling upward and downward,
then, by means of specific substances, he becomes fit for the elixir of mercury (rasāyana).
Or else, cast into the lamp-machine, he is liberated from all defects.
The king of alchemical mercury (sūtarāja), having been cast down by the method of horizontal precipitation,
is likewise combined with finely ground mica-leaf and sour gruel (āranāla).
Having placed it on the mortar and crushed it until it reaches the state of lost powder,
one should gradually apply a firm fire to the mercury that has been cast down by the transverse-pouring method.
This [metal] is to be heated and cast; as long as it does not fall when [thrown] into the fire while still solid, then that ore is purified and will certainly become fit for work.
Through *mardanas*, *mūrchanās*, and *pātas*, the dull sentiment (*rasa*) becomes tranquil.
Then, by means of creation with lotuses and restraint, the mercury (rasa) produces a face;
through the power of sweating and other processes, the elixir (sūta) attains unsurpassed potency (vīrya).
Then, for the sake of properly restraining that [mind] and turning it away from fickleness,
one should prepare a paste of *karkoṭī*, the eyes of a serpent, scorpion, lotus,
and *mārkava* together with sour gruel (*āranāla*), and subject it to fomentation for three days.
By means of Marica combined with Bhūkhaga, along with Lavaṇa, Āsurī, Śigru, and Ṭaṅkaṇa,
and mixed with sour gruel (kāñjika) for three days, one becomes capable of consuming food through the process of sweating.

That which has been processed with the three alkalies (trikṣāra), rock salt, saltpeter, borax, copper sulfate, long pepper, ginger, black pepper, and the like— along with pungent, salty, and sour substances such as *amlavetasa*— and then dried in a copper vessel from Nepal using fermented gruel (*māranāla*), is a digestive stimulant when combined with sour fermented liquors (*amlāsava*).
One should apply sudation with fermented sour gruel (āsava) to increase the power and vigor;
furthermore, one should be subjected to sudation according to necessity with the juices of medicinal roots.
Sarpākṣī, Kṣīriṇī, Vandhyā, Matsyākṣī, Śaṅkhapuṣpikā,
Kākajaṅghā, Śikhiśikhā, Brahmadaṇḍī, and Ākhukarṇikā.
Varṣābhū, kambukī, dūrvā, sairyaka, utpala, śimbikā,
śatāvarī, vajralatā, vajrakanda, and agnikarṇikā.
White arka, śigru, dhattūra, mṛga, dūrvā, rasāṅkuśa, rambhā, red-colored nirguṇḍī, lajjālu, and suradālikā.
Maṇḍūkaparṇī, pātālī, citraka, grīṣmasundarā, kākamācī, mahārāṣṭrī, haridrā, and tilaparṇikā.
Jātī, jayantī, the goddess Śrī, bhūkadamba, kusumbhaka, kośātakī, water, kaṇā, lāṅgalī, and kaṭutumbikā.
Cakramarda, amṛtā, kanda, puṅkhikā among the sūryāvartas,
vārāhī, and hastiśuṇḍī are generally medicinal plants used for their juices.
These eight purificatory processes of mercury—namely, *bhāvanā*, *sveda*, *mṛd*, *ālepa*, and the others—are highly esteemed; they are applied equally to the substance for the purpose of *rasāyana*.
These should be performed first, whereas the remaining processes useful for medicinal substances have not been mentioned here.

We shall now describe twenty-five types of mercury-binding (rasabandha), for it is by means of these that the volatility and the difficulty of grasping of the king of essences (rasarāja) are destroyed; this is indeed what has been proclaimed by the Vārttikas for the purpose of binding.
Haṭha, āroṭa, as well as ābhāsa, kriyāhīna, piṣṭikā, kṣāra, khoṭa, poṭa, kalkabandha, and kajjali; // VRrs_11.61 //
It is both with life and without life, seedless and with seed;
it consists of chains and the binding of the limbs, as well as the infant and the youth.
The youthful, the aged, the one bound in form, another, the water-bond, the fire-bond, that which is called well-refined, and that called the great bond— these are declared to be twenty-five.
Some say that the twenty-sixth [posture], known as *jalūkābandha*, is not intended for the body; it is highly praised, however, for the arousal of women.
That which is devoid of complete purification should be known as "forceful" (haṭha) mercury;
when consumed by men, it may cause either death or a violent disease.
Mercury that has been thoroughly purified is correctly called *āroṭa*;
it is excellent for the purpose of "field-making" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*) and gradually destroys diseases.
The essence that, being enclosed, enters into union while abandoning its own nature,
becomes a manifestation through the cultivation of the elements, roots, and so forth, due to the transformation of its qualities.

That best of elixirs which is prepared with impure iron and other such substances should be known as deficient in its efficacy; it undergoes adverse transformation when unwholesome [substances] are consumed.
Under intense heat, through thorough pressing, it becomes a paste in the form of butter;
that essence, bound as a paste, is highly stimulating and digestive.
That mercury which has been processed with conch shells, pearl oysters, cowrie shells, and so forth, is a "bound alkali" (kṣārabandha); it produces supreme luster and nourishment, and destroys colic.
That which becomes a solid mass when bound, and goes to destruction as it is repeatedly smelted, should be known as *khoṭabandha*; it quickly removes all diseases.
Molten lampblack, flattened upon a plantain leaf, forms a paste known as *parpaṭī*;
this very preparation cures all diseases, such as those of children.

The mercury (sūta), having been processed by means of sweating and other methods and having attained the state of a paste (paṅka), is to be known as "bound by a paste" (kalkabaddha); it bestows the fruits declared in the [relevant] yoga.
Kajjalī is produced from mercury and sulfur; it is very smooth and resembles collyrium.
When combined with various specific formulations, it is called kajjalī-bandha.
When reduced to ashes through the application of fire, the mercury becomes truly endowed with life;
when properly utilized, it does not produce the effect of mere ash, but swiftly brings about the destruction of diseases.
Whether it be aged *abhraka* or one whose scent has completely vanished, once all the metals have been reduced to ashes,
that mercury-ash known as "Lifeless" (*nirjīva*) instantly destroys all diseases without exception.
When mercury has been digested with one-fourth part of its weight in mineral colorants (varṇa) and processed into a paste through the addition of sulfur,
and is then subjected to successive *puṭa* (herbivore-fire) treatments with equal parts of sulfur, it becomes known as "seedless" (*nirbīja*) mercury, which destroys all diseases.
That [mercury] which has been thoroughly roasted with powdered mica-essence, gold, copper,
and iron, and then killed with six times its weight of sulfur, becomes bound with seed (sabījabaddha) and possesses immense power.
Mercury struck by a diamond and so forth is "struck mercury" (hata-sūta); it is not equal to the other [types].
But mercury bound in chains (śṛṅkhalābaddha) brings about the transformation of the body and metals;
Śaṅkara alone knows its manifold power and its rapid pervasion.

Even if the mercury (sūta) has undergone liquefaction with external fluxes (*druti*) or has reached a state of fixation (*bandha*), yet remains in the form of ash, it destroys even most difficult-to-cure diseases when applied in a dose of one-quarter of a *rājikā* seed; this is known as "bound by flux" (*drutibaddha*).
But the child born of Śiva, when properly served and joined with yoga, becomes aged like a cloud;
it is a swift elixir (*rasāyana*) that removes future diseases and destroys even those afflictions accompanied by calamities and fatal signs.

That which is born from mercury (harodbhava), when processed for twice the duration of a cloud-cycle (dviguṇābhrajīrṇa), becomes Kumāra; it consists of measured rice-grains and, after twenty-one nights, truly destroys the multitude of sinful diseases and serves as an elixir (rasāyana).
This foremost elixir, known as Taruṇa, which consumes four parts of mercury and one part of mica, destroys all diseases within seven nights; it is an elixir that bestows vigor and strength.
He for whom sixfold abhraka has been digested and who has attained friendship with fire is indeed named Vṛddha;
he should be employed in both the body and in metal—who, other than Śiva, can describe his qualities?

The mercury that has been processed with divine roots and rendered capable of enduring intense fire becomes a great mercury (*mahārasa*) through the "molding bond" (*mūrtibandha*), even without the preliminary process of digestion by means of mica (*abhrajāraṇā*).
For this elixir, even when being consumed by fire, is not diminished;
when employed in all medicinal preparations, it bestows incomparable fruits.
Bound by waters flowing from the mouths of stone-fountains, this [place] possesses water-bonds;
it destroys old age, disease, and death, and bestows the fruits described in the Kalpas.
Or, when blown alone within the yogas, it may take the form of a pill;
bound by fire, it is indeed imperishable and brings about such states as the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva).
With *viṣṇukrāntā*, *śaśilatā*, the roots of *kumbhī* and *kanaka*, with *viśālā*, *nāginī*, the tubers of *vyāghrapādī*, and *kuruṇṭaka*; 11.89.
One should grind *vṛścikālī*, *bhaśuṇḍī*, and *haṃsapādā* together with the urine of cows that have not yet calved, or cook them in *kulaka*.
In this manner, having ground the mercury with metals that have been calcined, one should cook it in apparatus;
this is the method for the fainting (mūrchā) of mercuries in brief.
When heated together with gold or silver, it attains a state of oneness; it is unyielding, dense, heavy, and shaped like a pill, yet exceedingly long and brilliant.
When struck and rubbed, it turns to powder like cloth and does not shed its impurity; odorless, it melts in an instant—this indeed is the mercury known as Mahābandha.
When half a part of gold is combined with lead (nāga) in the proportion of one-fourth, or alternatively with five parts of *uṣṭhaka*, *śālmalī*, *madāśleṣmāta* seeds,
and likewise with the powder derived from the fruits known as *tejinī* and *kolaka*, and these are placed upon a heated mortar and rubbed, the excellent *jalūkā* [elixir] is produced.

This very *jalūkā*—which is *kapikacchū* in its mass of hair, *candrāvatī* in its oil, and *tejini* when soaked in a liquid of *ṭaṅkaṇa*, *kāma*, and *pippalī*—should be rubbed with effort according to the prescribed method on a heated stone slab; the pill (*vaṭī*) thus prepared is renowned as the best for destroying the intoxication and pride of women.
In childhood, an eight-finger length [of leech] should be applied; in youth, ten fingers;
and for those who are mature, twelve. Thus, the leech is considered to be of three kinds.
Having placed the vessel at the mouth of a goat, one should cause it to be filled with ewe’s milk;
then one should set it in the intense heat of the sun for twenty-one days.
The second [mudrā] described here by me is beneficial for the liquefaction of the leech;
situated upon the head of men, it wondrously causes the seed to flow.
One should also take the juice from the leaves of the *muni* plant, water from the whorls of the *śālmalī* tree,
and water from the roots of the *jātī* jasmine combined with water from the *śiṃśapā* tree.
The wise one should grind together the fruit of the *śleṣmātaka*, the powder of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), the powder of *kokilākṣa*, and mercury.
A divine leech is produced that is enchanting to the minds of women;
it should be applied at the time of passion, and the woman herself shall desire him.
Lead that has been processed with equal proportions of triphalā, bhṛṅga, and mahauṣadha, along with honey, ghee, goat’s milk, and cow urine,
and subjected to seven immersions, becomes *jalūkā* when it has been fused with mercury.
One should purify the copper, measured by the number of days in the solar month, with the juice of *aṅkola*, *rājavṛkṣaka*, and *kanyā*. 11.102.
One should thoroughly rub together the powders of śaśirekhā, varavarṇinī, sakokilākṣā, apāmārga, and kanaka for twenty-one days.
Having administered sour gruel (*kāñjika*) or broth at night, one should introduce it into the vagina;
this should be applied according to the sequence for young, middle-aged, and old women after identifying their respective stages.
Even for men who are devoid of passion, a woman will become eager for union.
Take four parts of mercury, five parts of tin,
an equal amount of *surasāra*, and combine them with *ṭaṅkaṇa*.
Having ground that ball produced from mercury for three days,
when it is placed at the tip of the linga within the yoni, it brings one under control for as long as one lives.
Having sprinkled the *nāga* with camphor, *sūraṇa*, *subhṛṅga*, and *sumeghanāda*, one should encircle it with the resulting juice.
By wearing this ring upon the penis, a man becomes the daily master and the very source of life for women of shapely hips.
By applying a paste made of ṭaṅkaṇa, pippalī, sūraṇa, karpūra,
and the juice of mātuluṅga to her own liṅga, one may cause the vulva of women to dilate.
Then, having placed the seed of Hara (the letter *ha*) upon the serpent turned by fire (*agni*), one should double it;
then, with the sage (*muni*), gold (*kanaka*), serpent (*nāga*), and snake (*sarpa*), one should grind it with *dantī* and sprinkle that mixture.
Having ground the *madanavālaka* with buttermilk, one should prepare a powder;
at the time of sexual union, it destroys the pride of passion in women.
The juice of *vyāghrī* and *bṛhatī* fruits, *sūraṇa* tuber, and sour chickpea leaves; and the powder of *kapikacchu*, *vajravallī*, long pepper (*pippalī*), and tamarind (*amlīkā*).
One should grind the naga-plant (nāga) that has been processed by fire nine times with cooling substances;
having fashioned this into a ring for the god of love, it causes women to melt with passion.
The seed of the *palāśa* tree, mercury, and the juice of the sour *raktajambīra* fruit, when ground together with "life" (*sajīva*) and heated in a vessel, certainly dies [is killed]. (VR 11.113)
Having prepared a paste with finely powdered seeds of *kharamañjarī* and lotus seeds (*puṣkara*), one should strongly roast the mercury in a sealed crucible; it will become ash.
Indeed, asafoetida well-purified with the milk of the *kākodumbarikā* plant reduces mercury to ash through the procedures of rubbing and encapsulation.
One should grind *devadālī* and *harikrāntā* with the juice of *āranāla*;
with that liquid, one should subject mercury (*sūta*) to seven cycles of being rubbed and made to swoon.
One should place its juice in an earthen pan and, having poured it out again and again, cook that liquid over a stove during the day; it will become an ash resembling salt.

One should grind the seeds of *apāmārga* as well as those of *eraṇḍa*; that powder should be placed within mercury, positioned one above the other in a crucible. Having sealed it, one should cook it with four small *puṭas* and reduce it to a state of ash.
The mercury, having been steamed seven times with a bulbous root grown from a bitter gourd that has been soaked in a woman’s milk, is killed by a fire of cow dung.

One should grind mercury combined with sulfur in a mortar with water from the roots of the *aṅkola* plant; at the end of the day, one should seal it and subject it to heating in a *bhūdharayantra*. At the end of the day, it becomes dead [mercury]. // VRrs_11.120 //
One should grind mercury and iron with the milky sap of the *vaṭa* tree for three *praharas*;
by means of that wood, one should cook it, and that mercury will be reduced to ashes.
Then the afflicted man [should approach] the master of mercury, who is Maheśvara himself in visible form,
and the prepared mercury held in a horn, tooth, bamboo tube, or other vessel.
Having honored the gods, cows, and Brahmins according to one's ability,
one should eat the juice held in a leaf-cup, followed by water as a drink.
[The soup] prepared with ghee, rock salt, coriander, cumin, and fresh ginger;
and [the vegetables] such as *taṇḍulīyaka*, coriander, *paṭola*, and *alambuṣā*.
Well-digested śāli rice, cow’s milk, ghee, curd,
*haṃsodaka* water, and mung bean soup— in brief, these constitute the category of wholesome foods.
Bṛhatī, bilva, kūṣmāṇḍa, the tips of vetra,
kāravellaka, māṣa, masūra, niṣpāva, kulattha, mustard seeds, and sesame.

One should strictly avoid jumping, rubbing the body with powders, bathing, copper vessels, wine, fermented liquors, the meat of marshy animals, sour gruel, eating from plantain leaves or bronze vessels, heavy foods, those that cause constipation, and anything excessively sharp or hot. 11.127.

The fruit of *kaṇṭārī*, sour gruel (*kāñjika*), tortoise oil, as well as black mustard, lime, *kataka* nut, *kaliṅgaka* fruit, pumpkin, cucumber, *kārī*, the fruit of *kukkuṭa* and *kāravella*, the fruit of *karkoṭikā*, eggplant, and wood-apple—this indeed is declared to be the group of items beginning with the letter *ka*. (VR 11.128)
This group beginning with the letter *ka* is considered as taught in the *Devīśāstra*;
however, that which is specified in other scriptures is now described according to another method.
Kaṅgu, kanduka, kola, kukkuṭa, kala, kroḍa, kulattha, as well as kaṇṭārī, kaṭutaila, kṛṣṇagala, tortoise,
kalāya, kaṇā, karkāru, kaṭhillaka, kataka, karkoṭaka, karkaṭī, kālī, kāñjika, and the group beginning with eṣaka— these have been declared by the illustrious Lord Kṛṣṇa.

In whichever rasa the letter *ka* and so forth are explicitly prohibited by direct statement, in each such case that [specific letter] is to be avoided; its propriety [is determined] from other sources.
When there is vomiting, one should eat rice with curd, black fish, and cumin;
in the event of agitation caused by wind (vāta), one should perform an oil massage using *nārāyaṇa* and other such oils.
In cases of aversion [to food], one should sprinkle cool water over the head;
in thirst, coconut water or mung beans with sugar [are recommended].
One should consume the fruits of the grape, pomegranate, date,

and banana for the purpose of increasing the essence and potency [of the body]. Furthermore, in the procedure for abandoning the taste, one should employ curd, milk, sugarcane, and sugar, as well as other cooling treatments.
One should eat *bṛhatī* and *bilva*; this is the general rule.
[It is indicated] for fever, hemorrhagic disease, cough, asthma and dyspnea,
hoarseness, consumption, as well as for anorexia and excessive salivation.
And also for vomiting and heart disease, for thirst, alcohol-induced disorders, and hemorrhoids;
for upward-moving wind (udāvarta), diarrhea, abdominal disorders of the small intestine (grahaṇī), and dysentery (pravāhikā).
[It is the remedy] for cholera, sluggish digestion, dysuria, urinary stones,
urinary disorders, somaroga, pustules, and abscesses.
For diseases such as enlargement of the spleen and abdominal tumors, for colic pains and abdominal enlargements, for jaundice, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, vitiligo, and skin ailments caused by wind.
[It is indicated] for those with obstructed or vitiated blood due to wind (vātāsra), for the sterile, for those suffering from diseases of pregnancy,
for postpartum women, for diseases of children, and also for insanity and epilepsy.
In diseases of the eyes, diseases of the ears, diseases of the nose and mouth,
in diseases arising in the head, in wounds, fractures, and fistula-in-ano;
For tumors and the like, minor diseases, secret ailments, and poisons;
for old age and for those without offspring, it serves as a means for nourishing the seed.
Indeed, the entire medical treatment for diseases follows this sequence; herein, I shall describe the formulations using juices, metals, and poisons according to the traditional scriptures.
Horripilation, trembling, sweetness in the mouth, yawning, aching in the head, and a burning sensation—
these indeed are said to be the symptoms of a fever caused by wind (vāta-jvara), provided they persist constantly after eating.

Purgation, dryness of the mouth, pungency, intense heat, delirium, vertigo, and fainting—these are the characteristics of fever caused by *pitta*, as are vomiting, thirst, and a burning sensation in the limbs. (VR 12.10)
Cough, dyspnea, numbness of the mouth, sweetness in the mouth,
excessive sleepiness, perspiration, and slight burning sensation are the characteristics of fever born of phlegm (kapha).
That characteristic which is mixed belongs to both or to all three.
One should form a ball from mercury and sulfur that have been thoroughly rubbed together with water;
having placed it inside a new vessel, one should subsequently place a copper plate over that ball.
Having suppressed it for half a moment, the wise one should kindle his blazing fire from below; then this medicinal paste is perfected, acting as a cloud to extinguish the forest fire of acute fever.
Having first smeared the tongue and the region of the palate with Sindhu-born salt and moist cumin,
one should apply this [powder] in the measure of a *valla*, mixed with fresh ginger juice, and cover it with a cloth.
From this point forward, even beyond the onset of perspiration, buttermilk and rice are to be used as wholesome food;
if one proceeds in this manner for three days, then what need would there even be for any suspicion of fever?

Equal parts of mercury, copper, sulphur, mercury-cinnabar, *jayapāla*, *tiktā*, *pathyā*, *trivṛt*, and *viṣatinduka* should be processed with the milk of a *vajrī* cow; this "elixir of the three worlds," taken with honey in three grains, destroys even recent fever.
One-fourth part of *sāra-ravi*, an equal portion of *gandha*, and well-matured [medicinal herbs] ground with their own decoction—
this liquid, measured by the sequence of one *māṣa* each for fevers caused by wind (*anila*) and the other humors, is indeed known by the name Meghanāda.
One should give two *valla* of well-ground pure mercury (*sūta*) along with sulphur (*gandha*), mixed with *darada* (cinnabar) and water, for one period of three hours (*prahara*).

This medicine, known as "The Lion for the Elephant of Fever" (*jvaragajaharin*), should be taken with ginger water; one who suffers from the burning sensation produced at the onset of fever should eat with milk and rice.
One should also mix mercury with heated lead, along with sulphur and long pepper,
each in equal parts, there according to the prescribed method.
One should grind everything for three days in the juice of *jambīra*,
and likewise for three days in the juice of *meghanāda* and *kumārī*.
One should soak [the ingredients] for two days in goat’s urine and for three days in cow’s urine;
then, one should add these [other substances] to it as appropriate.
Having combined one part of rock salt (*saindhava*), one part of *citraka*, and likewise one part of black salt (*sauvarcala-lavaṇa*),
one should saturate [the mixture] with [the liquid] again and again.
By this method, that medicinal juice becomes properly perfected;
one should administer three *valla*s of the juice combined with sugar and clarified butter.
Boiled rice made from wheat, along with mung bean soup and *vāstuka* greens,
combined with *dhātrī* fruit, destroys all fevers;
this is proclaimed by those learned in the tantras as "Dīpikā-rasa."
Mercury, green vitriol, orpiment, blue vitriol, sulphur, and borax— all these, purified and in equal parts, should be macerated for one day with the juices of *kāravallī*.
One should rub that paste and smear it on the inner surface of a copper vessel to a thickness of one-eighth of an inch; then, one should heat it in a bed of sand.
When the grains of rice placed upon his back have thus burst open within the apparatus,
the physician should then extract the well-cooled [substance] from the interior of the copper vessel.
The elixir named Śītabhañjī should be powdered together with black pepper;
one should consume one *māṣa* of it with a leaf-fragment, and it will destroy fever—
whether irregular, acute, or occurring on the first, second, third, or fourth day— within three days.
One should grind equal parts of mercury, mica, and realgar with the juice of karkaṭī;
having placed that paste, reduced to the consistency of collyrium, into a copper vessel, [one should proceed].
Then, having processed it in a sand-press according to the prescribed method,
the best of physicians should administer a dose of one *māṣa* with powdered black pepper.
In the case of a cold-fever (śītajvara), one should drink a handful of warm water;
this is the "Cold-Breaker" (śītabhañjī) elixir, which wards off cold-fever.
Having thoroughly purified talc with the powder of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and sesame oil, and having ground it intensely with an equal amount of *suṣavī* juice,
one should form a ball with mercury produced from cinnabar inside a crucible known as the "sand-oven" (*sikatāyantra*) situated between two inverted lids.
Having covered that [substance] with a leaf and sealed the junction of the two with jaggery, lime, and *khaṭikā* (chalk) mixed with *śivā* (myrobalan),
the wise man should cook it over a gentle fire until the mere discoloration of the rice placed atop the vessel serves as the limit.
Then one should give him *valla* mixed with *surasā*, followed by ghee, sugar, water, and honey as a drink.
To conquer even virulent fevers here, and for the sake of pacifying vomiting, one should pour a stream of very cold water over the head.

Then [he saw] that king of elixirs, the crest-jewel adorning the head of mercury, known as "the reviver of the dead," by which there might be an instantaneous restoration of life for the sick, as if by the essence of nectar.
One *guñjā* of mercury, vermilion, and *jepāla*, increased in dose and rubbed with the juice of *dantī*, destroys fever when taken with sugar after half a day.
One should grind together purified mercury, poison, sulfur, and datura seeds in equal parts, along with an amount of the three pungents (vyoṣa) equal to those four, and store the resulting powder.
It should never be administered in an ivory vessel, nor in a horn, nor in wood;
it may be given in cases of fever caused by wind and phlegm, by a combination of two humors, or by all three humors.
With the juice of ginger or else of jambīra, one should take two guñjās; once this has been digested, one should consume curd with rice.
This elixir, named Mahājvarāṅkuśa, proclaimed by Śambhu, shall destroy fevers according to the sequence of the humors within one, two, or three days.

Having ground together *tāla*, copper dust, mercury, *gagana*, Nepalese *gandhaka*, one *dīnāra* of *ṭaṅka* (cinnabar), half that amount of *śilājatu* and *mākṣika*, and two *dīnāras* of *viṣa* (aconite) with the juices of *śikhin*, it is cooked; this [preparation], which conquers floods of fever like the *cintāmaṇi* jewel, is known by the name *Mṛtyuñjaya*.

Equal parts of *tāla* (orpiment), copper, iron filings, *capalā*, *tuttha*, mica, *kāntaka*, and lead, along with well-ground *paunarnava* root, should be made into a paste with the juices of *bhṛṅgī*, *kāsaharī*, *punarnavā*, and the leaves of *mahāmandāra*; when cooked in a *vālukāyantra*, this cures all fevers.

The fragrance born of Śiva is equal to nutmeg; it should be rubbed with the juice of a citron for three days. Mix with that an equal amount of the three pungents (vyoṣa); from that, Candrasūrya is perfected.
To conquer fever that clings to the body, a leaf of the creeper known as *bhujaga* should be applied;
its milk is beneficial here when taken with the juice of ginger, and it should be employed for cooling purposes.
But for fever with internal complications and colic, buttermilk is beneficial; the remedy mentioned immediately above [is taken] with grape water.
Colic is relieved by *rodhra* with the water of *varā*, or by *varā* and water with the juice of *jambīra*.
In this case of epilepsy (apasmṛti), an ointment made from the milk-exudation of the *bimba* tree should be applied;
here, ghee with boiled rice should be used for food, and it destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) when taken with the juice of the *jambīra* fruit.
In cases of splenic enlargement (plīhodara), one should administer [medicines] with the juice of *hiṅgu*, *amlīkā*, and *nimbu*, followed by a meal of rice with buttermilk.
For the purpose of arresting [the disease], milk mixed with sugar should be taken; molasses should be employed for the pacification of vomiting.
Poison should not be given to one who is eighty years of age, nor to one whose wealth has been exhausted; if it were given, it would cause harm.
One should prepare these in equal parts: *megha*, *pārada*, *gandhāśman*, *viṣa*, *vyoṣa*, *paṭu*, and the two types of *jīraka*.
One should also grind it for seven nights with the juice of *sinduvāra*, the juice of garlic, and the juice of *apāmārga*.

Once that has been processed in a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra), one should administer a dose of one guñjā, along with betel leaf and black pepper; thereafter, one should have the patient drink cold water.
The elixir named Umāprasādana removes cold fevers;
it destroys quartan and tertian fevers—how much more so other ailments?
One should take equal parts of borax, mercury, and sulfur,
and having added double the amount of Nepalese copper, one should grind them together within a mortar.
One should massage it gently until it attains smoothness;
[then add] rock salt, black pepper, conch-shell, and the alkali of tamarind, together with honey.
Having made this equal to that, one should then rub it with lime juice;
one should consume a pill the size of a chickpea for three days.
It destroys all fevers— those occurring every day, every two days, every three days, and every four days— and is thus known as the "Goad for Fever."
Having taken one *tolaka* each of mica, sulfur,
and mercury, and half a *tolaka* of poison, along with half a *tolaka* of tamarind fruit;
Having made all of this equal, one should grind it within the mortar;
one should grind it slowly until it reaches a state of smoothness.
Having dug a pit six finger-breadths deep in both width and circumference,
a man should cast the leaves of the *phaṇivallī* plant into the interior of that pit.
One should place that medicinal paste upon leaves firmly into a pit;
then, one should fill the mouth of the pit over the paste with those same leaves.
Then, one should place the powder into a pit along with wild blue lotuses;
once it has been known to have cooled to the temperature of one's own body, one should draw it out thereafter.
One should grind the paste together with leaves smeared with lac in a mortar,
adding half a *tola* of *amṛta* and half a *tola* of *tintiḍī* fruit.
One should set aside the prepared paste and administer it in a dose of one *guñjā*,
combined with ginger-water and the pungent substances *citraka* and rock salt.

It should likewise be administered in cases of fever caused by the combination of humors (saṃnipāta), by wind (vāta), or by all three humors (tridoṣa), as well as in irregular fevers (viṣamajvara), weak digestion (agnimāndya), chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī), and acute dysentery (atisāra).
One should prepare food consisting of curd and boiled rice with this broth;
then, according to the specific illness and other factors, one should pour water over it.
This glorious and supreme yoga bestows life upon living beings;
it is celebrated as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), a mercury beautiful in every limb.

Having thoroughly rubbed the lord of mercury (sūtendra) with the five pungent substances (pañcapaṭu) and the three alkalis (kṣāra), one should then subject it to sweating within a mass (piṇḍa) composed of asafoetida (hiṅgu), great medicinal herbs (mahauṣadha), and wine (asurī), using a decoction of grains (dhānyodaka).
Then, [it should be treated] with waters derived from nirguṇḍī, fire (hutāśa), mantha, tilaparṇī, unmatta, bhṛṅga, fresh ginger (ārdraka), kāmatā, girikarṇikā, plava, dala, and pañcāṅgula.

Having thoroughly ground it with equal parts of mercury and innate bile, one should then saturate it with the bile of fanged animals, goats, hyenas, fish, and peacocks; this will conquer *saṃnipāta* fevers.
Renowned on earth as the Lokanātha-guṭikā, it is beneficial in a dose the size of a black pepper (*mārīca*); when taken with curd and sugarcane pieces, its potency becomes cooling.
One *niṣka* each of the ashes of diamond (*vajra*) and vaikrānta,
two *niṣkas* of *śṛṅgī* poison, and three *niṣkas* of *cūlikāpaṭu*.
One should combine five niṣkas of agnijāra with everything else in one place; one should grind the ash and the mercury together for three days until the mixture reaches that consistency.
One should saturate the group of drugs beginning with śārṅgaṣṭā twenty-three times with alkaline water, then grind them and dry them thoroughly.
Then, having kneaded it for a day, one should place it in a tooth-casket;
this is the mercury known as *Mṛtasaṃjīvana*, an ornament for the needle.
For one who is about to die due to a violent complication and has fallen to the ground,
one should then extract this essence from the palate by piercing it.
Then, having pierced it with an extremely fine needle that has been thoroughly cleansed with water and carefully smeared it with oil, one should place it in a windless location.
Then, more than half a watch later, having discharged his urine and excrement, he regained consciousness; though filled with vigor, he repeatedly shook his head.
One should recognize that the venerable one has indeed changed from one state to another;
then, one should place him in a cauldron filled with cold water.
There, having removed the boiled water, one should add another;
then, to that person who is begging, one should afterwards give milk mixed with sugar to drink.
One should offer curd mixed with sugar, coconut water, and plantains; otherwise, he will surely die.
When he had regained consciousness and was speaking, begging for fruits and such,
[the king] dragged him away from there, rubbed him with oil, and squeezed out the oil.
One should apply ointments of fragrant substances and camphor from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head;
thus, one should treat [the patient] with such cooling substances for seven nights.
On the arrival of the eighth day, one should repeatedly apply the juice derived from the root of the *dardurī* plant to the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth, using a boat as a support.
One should administer it with sugar to bring down the morbid humor;
once the humor has been brought down, one may afterwards give food and curd as desired.
Accompanied by inhalation and exhalation, and other signs of life having been restored,
one should place him in a cauldron filled with water for the sake of regaining consciousness.
Having drawn in that one who has attained awakening, one should treat him as before;
he lives out his full lifespan and dies immediately thereafter.
Even Brahmā cannot find the end of that Dharma which rescues one sinking into the most terrible confluence, the ocean of death.
A person who has been liberated from the great fear of death caused by the convergence of humors should honor the physician for saving his life even with the gift of all his possessions.
"Otherwise, one remains in hell for as long as the eons are reckoned"—
this is the command of Śaṅkara, proclaimed by Śambhu.
The elucidation based on the extraction of aesthetic flavor (rasa) must never be performed by the dull-witted who,
out of a desire for wealth, impart it without the authority of the scriptures; rather,
having obtained the grace of the Guru, let it be applied during the assembly.
Śārṅgaṣṭā, as well as vyāghrī, karīra, tilaparṇikā, indravāruṇikā, mustā, haridrā, and the root of aṅkola; VR 12.90.
Apāmārga, kaṇā, gold, kaṭutumbī, and tintiḍī—
this group beginning with śārṅgaṣṭā is a supreme remedy for the destruction of *saṃnipāta* disorders.

Having made a firm kajjalikā (collyrium paste) from equal parts of mercury, sulphur, talaka, realgar, cinnabar, orpiment, tutthaka, jepāla, poison, ṭaṅkaṇa, and madhuphala, one should saturate it with the bile of a snake of virulent poison; having cast this excellent mercury into a lead crucible, it is known by the name Sūcīmukha.

At the opening of Brahma, where drops of blood are scattered, one should give a single guñjā seed; having given it when there is a wind from a bowstring bound in a casket, accompanied by frost on the branches, one instantly conquers cough, asthma, loss of appetite, delirium, trembling, those afflicted by hiccups, muteness, deafness, insanity, epilepsy, and madness.
Mercury, sulfur, copper, and mica; lāṅgalī, fire (citraka), and asafoetida;
and the leaves of vandhyākarkoṭakī, paṭola, nirguṇḍī, sugandhā, and nimba.
One should grind together the three alkalies (pāṭhā), kṣāra, kṣāratraya, kṣveḍa, bola, dhattūra, taṇḍula, śṛṅgī, and the essence of madhuka with the acidic juice of jambīra.
One should indeed prepare pills with a measure of one niṣka;
that pill subdues fever accompanied by sweating and burning sensations, acting as a goad for the elephant of *saṃnipāta*.

The Vaiṣṇava army is indeed in the cycle of transmigration; it is immovable, adorned with the *kādi* [consonants] as its bracelets, endowed with passion like that of Rudra, mature, and graced with a head.
One should know that there are three parts of orpiment (tālaka) and one part of mercury (pārada); half of that [mercury] is sulphur (gandhaka), and half of that again is realgar (manaḥśilā).
One should grind that for three praharas with the juice of *kāravallī* leaves;
when cooked in a *vālukāyantra*, this elixir (*rasa*) cures quartan fever.
Sulfur, joined with mercury, becomes very beautiful;
it is tripled with *hiyāvalī* and rubbed with the juice of *nirguṇḍī*.
That [powder] should be applied seven times with the juice of fresh ginger;
it destroys continuous and other types of fever, acting as a goad for the elephant of quartan fever.
Realgar, orpiment, red arsenic, manahshila, copper, and sulphur, together with mercury, should be rubbed with the juice of musali;
when cooked in the "hen's egg" (kukkuṭī) puṭapāka method, it is known as Mṛtyuñjaya.
One should employ two *vallās* of this great elixir as desired with a meal of curd; it destroys acute fever and *saṃnipāta*. (VR 12.103)
One should grind purified mercury, poison, sulfur, black pepper, borax,
and long pepper with the juice of *dhūrta* seeds for one day, and then dry it.
The five-faced substance called *rasa*, weighing two *guñjās*, conquers the *saṃnipāta* fever;
one should administer it with a decoction of *arka* root along with *tryūṣaṇa*.
Curd-rice is beneficial in this case, and one should also employ the application of water.
One should grind mercury and sulphur in equal parts with the juice of *dhattūra* fruits for one day, and then add an equal amount of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*). This elixir,
known by the name Unmatta, conquers *saṃnipāta* when used as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
One should grind ten *niṣkas* of seed derived from *jepāla* (castor) free of its husk;
one should then mix it with one *niṣka* each of black pepper, long pepper, and mercury.
It should be soaked with the juices of *jambīra* for seven days with great care;
when used as an ointment, it quickly destroys *saṃnipāta* and is known as the auspicious (*śiva*) remedy.
Having powdered two *pratiniṣkas* each of *madanaphala*, *viḍalavaṇa*,
and mustard seeds, along with *ṭaṅkaṇa*, one should drink it with a decoction of *triphalā*.
In cases of skin disease, fever, jaundice, throat ailments, and indigestion,
one should take a single seed of *girikarṇī* with cold water as a nasal drop (*nasya*).
Having prepared a beautiful ink from two palas each of pure mercury and sulfur, one should add three *prakuñcas* of *mlecchalulāya*, *locana*, *manaḥśilā*, and *dhātrī*;
three *badara*-sized pieces of *pathyā*, six *śāṇas* of the three pungents (*tri-kaṭu*), *vacā*, *dharmiṇī*, *vellā*, *ambhodhara-pattraka*, *dvirada-kiñjalka*, and *aśvagandhā*.

Having ground all these ingredients together in equal proportions and weighing one *karṣa*, one should place them in a mortar and rub them thoroughly with half a *karañja* fruit, nectar (*amṛta*), *agasti*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*).

Then, with a steady mind, one should perform seven successive saturations (*bhāvanā*) using each of the following individually: *bhūdhātrī*, *vijayā*, the fruit of the ocean-born tree (*saritpatiphala*), *jvālāmukhī*, and *mārkava*.

Then, having prepared five types of *pitta* with the five [ingredients], the excellent physician should next fumigate it with *karañja* leaves and *amṛta*; then, having applied fresh ginger juice, he should fashion a pill in the shape of a grain of rice.

One part of *deya* (the base salt) should be given in cases of *saṃnipāta*; with *pratihataviṣaya*, it is used for the sleep of the eyes caused by delusion; with *ajamodā*, it is used for abdominal tumors (*gulma*); and with *tryūṣaṇa*, it is used for disorders of wind (*pavana*) and for chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*).
To protect the lives of elephants, horses, and men, Vaidyanātha declared that this *kāyāmbhodhi* should be administered along with an equal amount of *rasaka*.
The mercury, equal in quantity to sulphur and mica,
should be rubbed with the juice of Vārāhī and cooked in a *vālukāyantra* with *triphalā*, *vyoṣa*, and *citraka*.
Combined with the three alkalis, the five salts, asafoetida, guggulu, dīpyaka, cumin, and indrayava,
each in equal proportions with the meat broth.
A dose of one māṣa, taken with two palas of warm water as an after-drink, is for those suffering from fainting,
loss of digestive fire, disorders of the small intestine, anemia, or abdominal tumors.
One should perform the preservation of life; therefore, it is known as the "Lord of Life" (Prāṇeśvara).
When a disease increases, its application twice is approved by physicians.
Rasāñjana, vyoṣa, kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar, orpiment, mica, cinnabar, kumbhī, agni, bhṛṅga, mārī, taṇḍulīyaka, and honey; VRs 12.119.
Having ground equal parts of *hastiśuṇḍī* and half as much *śivagandhaka* with moist water for three days, one should place it in a sealed jar and heat it over a sand-fire (*vālukāgni*).
One should add the water of *jaya*, *jambīra*, *nirguṇḍī*, and *cāṅgerī*;
having boiled it for fourteen days, one should grind it while moist and dry it.
This elixir named Mṛtasaṃjīvana, when consumed in the measure of one *valla*,
will swiftly conquer all diseases, such as *saṃnipāta* and others.
One part of mercury (rasa) is considered to be [the base], with sulphur (gandhaka) being twice that amount;
along with poison (viṣa), orpiment (tālaka), kaṅkuṣṭha, realgar (śilā), vermilion (hiṅgula), and iron (lohaka).
Fire, the three pungents (trikaṭu), bhṛṅgarāja, honey, mica, hastiśuṇḍī, poison, kumbhī, taṇḍulīyaka, and copper; VRs 12.124.
Taking one part of each of these individually,
one should powder them and macerate the mixture with the juice of fresh ginger for three days.
The juice of the citron (jambīra) should be taken, measured at three palas;
likewise, three palas each of the three myrobalans (triphalā) and of nirguṇḍī [should be taken].
One *pala* of the juice of *cāṅgerī* is prescribed;
having placed it in a glass flask and inserted it into the apparatus, one should proceed with diligence.
Having extracted [the juice] with fresh ginger extracts and having rubbed it, one should dry it;
this elixir known on earth as "The Resuscitator of the Dead" (Mṛtasaṃjīvana) should be administered in a dose of two *guñjā*s to dispel *saṃnipāta* fever.
One should grind together equal parts of tin, lead, mercury, Nepalese sulphur, copper, and poison with moist *rasa* (juice).
Furthermore, this mercury, rubbed with the juice of *nirguṇḍī* and *cāṅgerī*,
when administered in a dose of one *valla*, destroys *saṃnipāta*.
Having prepared a kajjalī by mixing one karṣa each of purified sulphur and mercury together, one should then form it into a pill (golaka).
Having placed it in a new vessel, one should conceal it with a copper dish;
having sealed that vessel firmly, one should then set it upon the fire.
Once the swelling has subsided as much as the bursting of a grain of rice, one should extract it while it is still cool to the touch;
this juice, known as *parpaṭikā*, should be administered in cases of acute fever (*navajvara*).
The physician should firmly cover the fever patient with three applications of ginger juice for three days, until perspiration arises.
For a person freed from fever, rice with buttermilk (takrabhakta) is wholesome;
this elixir called Navajvarāri is exceedingly rare.
This elixir is considered generally effective, and especially so for fever caused by Vāta.
Take equal parts of borax, mercury, sulfur, and black pepper;
grind them all together with the juice of *jambīra* for three days.
Having dried it and mixed it with sugar, one should saturate it with fish bile;
once saturated, that juice should be processed for three days with the fresh juice of ginger.

Three vallas of cool water should be given for drinking; buttermilk with boiled rice mixed with eggplant fruit is wholesome. This *jalamañjarī* elixir destroys all types of acute fevers (*navajvara*). (VRs 12.138)
One should cause the ashes of vessels that have been pierced by the neck of a beloved [animal] to be made;
mercury equal to that amount, along with sulfur and ṭaṅkaṇa, [should be mixed] with neem water.
Then, having ground that paste, one should rub it for three days again.
One should infuse this with fish bile equal in quantity to the juice;
for this is the perfected *kāntarasa*, to be administered in cases of recent fever by the best of physicians in appropriate doses, accompanied by a post-drink of ginger.
Having mixed mercury with equal parts of mercury-oxide (rasa), sulfur, tin (vaṅga), and mica (abhraka), one should then grind the mercury together with an equal amount of tin.
There, having combined [the ingredients] and ground them with *jambīra* juice in a vessel of fragrant clay, one should apply the general *puṭapāka* method; thus the mercury is perfected seven times.
Then, having processed it seven times with *kumārī*, *citraka*, jaggery,
and cumin, one should administer it once the fever has become chronic.
Through the application of a decoction of triphalā, it cures cough and asthma;
through the application of a decoction of amṛtā, it cures insanity and dhanurvāta.
Thus, this elixir named Candrodaya is the destroyer of diseases.
Lead, tin, mercury, copper, sulfur, and likewise borax, as well as Nepalese poison and yellow orpiment, all in equal parts.
Having ground everything together with banyan milk, one should form it into a ball;
that ball should be cooked inside a vessel over the flame of a lamp.
Having cooled that globe, one should rub it with *bhṛṅgarāja*;
one should also rub it repeatedly with the juice of fresh ginger.
One should administer small balls (*vaṭaka*) the size of a chickpea, moistened with juice;
this, in a dose of two *guñjā* seeds, removes chronic fever.
Take mercury, sulfur, and realgar in equal parts;
having ground them together, one should employ them with the juice of *karkoṭikā*.
Murāri is effective against acute fever; one *valla* of it,
taken with sugar and followed by a post-digestive drink (*anupāna*) of *taṇḍulīya* juice or even with sugar alone,
destroys new fevers forcefully in the measure of two *guñjās*.
